KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced the addition of twelve new Silver members, reinforcing the community’s focus on open, vendor-neutral infrastructure for running AI agents in production. CNCF’s newest members reflect that shift, bringing domain expertise and technology built to run agentic workloads on open, portable infrastructure. New Silver Members The following organizations have recently joined CNCF as Silver Members: Centron is a German cloud provider on a mission to make the cloud as simple and accessible as possible – for everyone. Its ccloud³ platform offers managed Kubernetes, virtual machines, S3 object storage, and GPU compute, operated entirely from centron’s own ISO 27001- and C5-certified, GDPR-compliant data center in Germany. CIQ is the founding support and services partner for Rocky Linux and a leading provider of Enterprise Linux infrastructure. CIQ delivers secure, performant software infrastructure for the full range of modern workloads. Global enterprises, government agencies, research institutions and supercomputing centers trust CIQ to run their most advanced workloads in production, from mission-critical environments to the systems behind major scientific and AI breakthroughs. Based in Seattle, the company works to close the gap between CVE disclosure and a deployed fix across base OS packages, language runtimes, and open source libraries. Paper Compute is an open intelligence platform for teams building AI agents. Its agent gateway handles model routing, inference policy, and zero-instrumentation telemetry with tapes, deployed in your own cloud. Radar is an open source Kubernetes interface for humans and AI agents that shows how everything in a live cluster connects, not just what’s in it. items.title: CNCF Welcomes CoreWeave as a Platinum Member to Further Open Source AI Infrastructure
items.summary: Investment underscores CoreWeave’s continued push to build open, cloud native infrastructure for production AI at scale Key Highlights CoreWeave has upgraded its CNCF membership to Platinum, deepening its ongoing engagement in the open source cloud native ecosystem. CoreWeave is a participant in the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program and a contributor to Kubernetes, Kueue, and llm-d. CNCF Platinum membership reinforces a shared commitment to open source collaboration, vendor-neutral innovation, and long-term ecosystem sustainability. SAN FRANCISCO — November 10, 2026 — The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced that CoreWeave has upgraded to a Platinum Member, reinforcing its commitment to advancing the open source technologies that power production AI infrastructure. As generative AI moves from research labs into production environments, platform engineering teams are confronting a new frontier of infrastructure challenges. CoreWeave’s upgraded membership reflects its belief that the tools needed to meet those challenges — from distributed inference to workflow orchestration — should be built in the open, alongside the broader cloud native community. “CoreWeave’s expanded commitment as a Platinum Member reflects the growing importance of open source cloud native infrastructure to production AI,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director, CNCF. “We are proud to welcome CoreWeave as CNCF advances the open standards and technologies needed to run AI workloads reliably and efficiently at scale.” The Platinum upgrade reflects a broader pattern of contributions CoreWeave has made across the CNCF landscape. In May 2025, CoreWeave joined Red Hat, IBM, Google, and NVIDIA as a founding contributor to llm-d, believing that production inference needed to be built in the open. That project is now a CNCF Sandbox project. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America this year, CoreWeave Principal Software Engineer Rita Zhang received the Lifetime Achievement Award for her work over the past decade shaping and supporting the Kubernetes and CNCF communities. CoreWeave is also a participant in the Certified Kubernetes AI Conformance Program, an initiative the company sees as an important step in aligning the community around shared standards that make deploying AI at scale more consistent and reliable. Additionally, CoreWeave is a contributor to Kubernetes and Kueue. “We built our cloud on Kubernetes to run some of the largest AI models in the world at production scale, and we learned a lot doing it,” said Shadi Saba, vice president, engineering, AI/ML at CoreWeave. “Now we are applying those lessons to large-scale training, production inference, and agentic workloads. Platinum membership is how we bring that experience back to the community, showing up in the working groups, helping define what AI on Kubernetes actually means, and making top-tier compute available to the open source projects the whole ecosystem depends on. Upgrading our membership helps us work with the community to define the standards for the next generation of AI.” To learn more about becoming a CNCF member, visit https://www.cncf.io/about/join/ . items.title: Open Cluster Management (OCM) becomes a CNCF Incubating Project
items.summary: The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) voted to accept Open Cluster Management as a CNCF incubating project . Open Cluster Management is an open source project that simplifies the management of Kubernetes clusters across cloud, on-premises, and edge environments. Using a hub-and-spoke architecture and open APIs, OCM enables organizations to manage cluster registration, application deployment, and workload placement across multiple clusters without relying on a proprietary control plane. “Reaching CNCF incubation validates the engineering rigor of our global maintainers and the growing adoption of OCM across large-scale production fleets,” said Mike Ng, Maintainer, Open Cluster Management. From an architecture perspective, what I’m proudest of is our commitment to a lightweight, modular foundation rather than a monolithic platform. Built in close alignment with Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster standards, our asynchronous pull model guarantees cluster autonomy without centralizing sensitive credentials on the hub. Just as importantly, our pluggable add-on framework turns OCM into an extensible substrate, making it effortless for other cloud-native projects to inherit multicluster capabilities without reinventing the plumbing. Looking ahead, we are focused on streamlining setup and onboarding while advancing progressive rollouts for safer workload delivery, ultimately keeping distributed Kubernetes simple, secure, and composable.” Open Cluster Management’s Milestones and Ecosystem Development As organizations grow beyond a handful of Kubernetes clusters across clouds, regions, edge locations, and teams, they have to register and onboard clusters, distribute applications and policies, keep configuration consistent, and recover from failures without disrupting running workloads. Open Cluster Management provides these capabilities through vendor neutral, declarative Kubernetes APIs, and its hub-and-spoke model is designed to survive the failure and recovery of components without interrupting workloads. Originally developed by IBM and Red Hat, Open Cluster Management joined the CNCF Sandbox in November 2021. Since reaching its 1.0 release in June 2025, the project has delivered four subsequent minor updates (up through 1.4 in October 2026), expanding its capabilities for multicluster management, application delivery, and observability. Key release highlights include: CEL-based cluster selection and an Argo CD pull model add-on (1.0) A gRPC-based hub-and-spoke connection, plus add-ons for Kueue MultiKueue and OpenTelemetry (1.1) Advanced Placement configuration, automated hosting cluster resolution, and the introduction of the argocd-agent integration to provide highly scalable multi-cluster GitOps and complete application status visibility (1.2) Enhancements to ManifestWork resource ordering and the graduation of the AddOnTemplate API to v1beta1 (1.3) Syncing OCM PlacementDecisions to SIG Multicluster’s PlacementDecision API, ManifestWork observability, and security hardening such as network policies (1.4) OCM works closely with the broader cloud native ecosystem. It implements and aligns with the Kubernetes SIG Multicluster APIs, supplies Argo CD with cluster decisions for GitOps deployments, and integrates with Cluster API for cluster lifecycle. KubeVela, KubeStellar, Kueue, and Meshery all document OCM integrations, and the project maintains add-ons and examples for Argo CD, Fluid, and OpenTelemetry. Twenty-seven maintainers from eight organizations, including Red Hat, Guidewire, eBay, AppsCode, and Spectro Cloud, lead the project. OCM has demonstrated adoption across organizations including Alibaba Cloud, AppsCode, Guidewire, Red Hat, and Spectro Cloud. At eBay, OCM supports application deployment across more than 190 Kubernetes clusters through integrations with Argo CD. Groww uses OCM to support progressive application rollouts, while VESSEL AI leverages the project to manage GPU clusters and distribute AI workloads across cloud environments. “As Kubernetes adoption expands across increasingly complex environments, organizations need open, interoperable approaches to managing clusters at scale,” said Karena Angell, CNCF Technical Oversight Committee member. “Open Cluster Management has demonstrated technical maturity, a growing contributor community, and meaningful adoption across the cloud native ecosystem. Its advancement to incubation reflects the project’s progress in helping organizations manage multicluster environments without relying on proprietary solutions.” Main Components Open Cluster Management’s main components consist of the following: Cluster Manager: The hub side control plane that coordinates registration, work, placement, and add-ons. Klusterlet: The agent on each managed cluster that registers it with the hub and applies instructions from it. Cluster Inventory (registration): Registers manage clusters through a double opt-in handshake and mTLS connection, with certificate rotation and a dedicated namespace per cluster on the hub. ManifestWork API: Distributes Kubernetes resources to managed clusters, with update strategies, conflict resolution, and status feedback. Agents pull work from the hub, so the hub does not store managed cluster credentials. Placement API: Dynamically selects clusters using labels, resource capacity, or custom criteria and publishes the result as a PlacementDecision that any scheduler or controller can consume. Add-on framework: A structure for projects to become multicluster aware, handling registration, lifecycle, configuration, and status reporting. clusteradm: A command line tool to bootstrap a hub and join clusters. Built-in extensions: Cluster API integration for cluster lifecycle, an Argo CD add-on for pull-based application delivery, and governance, risk, and compliance policy controllers. Notable Milestones 1,100 GitHub Stars 1,370 pull requests 537 contributors from 84 organizations across 16 countries CNCF-Hosted Projects The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) provides technical leadership to CNCF projects, overseeing their progression through maturity levels and supporting long-term sustainability. Projects advancing to incubation demonstrate growing adoption, technical maturity, and community development. As a CNCF-hosted project, Open Cluster Management is part of a neutral foundation aligned with its technical interests, as well as the larger Linux Foundation, which provides governance, marketing support, and community outreach. OCM joins incubating technologies Artifact Hub, Backstage, Chaos Mesh, Cloud Custodian, Container Network Interface (CNI), Contour, Cortex, Emissary-ingress, Fluid, gRPC, HAMi, k8gb, Keycloak, KServe, Kubescape, KubeVela, KubeVirt, Lima, Litmus, Longhorn, Meshery, metal3-io, Microcks, Notary Project, OpenCost, OpenFeature, OpenFGA, OpenKruise, OpenYurt, Operator Framework, Strimzi, Tekton, Thanos, Volcano, and wasmCloud. For detailed maturity requirements at each level, please visit the CNCF Graduation Criteria .

Just as importantly, our pluggable add-on framework turns OCM into an extensible substrate, making it effortless for other cloud-native projects to inherit multicluster capabilities without reinventing the plumbing. Looking ahead, we are focused on streamlining setup and onboarding while advancing progressive rollouts for safer workload delivery, ultimately keeping distributed Kubernetes simple, secure, and composable.”

Open Cluster Management’s Milestones and Ecosystem Development

As organizations grow beyond a handful of Kubernetes clusters across clouds, regions, edge locations, and teams, they have to register and onboard clusters, distribute applications and policies, keep configuration consistent, and recover from failures without disrupting running workloads. Open Cluster Management provides these capabilities through vendor neutral, declarative Kubernetes APIs, and its hub-and-spoke model is designed to survive the failure and recovery of components without interrupting workloads.

Originally developed by IBM and Red Hat, Open Cluster Management joined the CNCF Sandbox in November 2021. Since reaching its 1.0 release in June 2025, the project has delivered four subsequent minor updates (up through 1.4 in October 2026), expanding its capabilities for multicluster management, application delivery, and observability. Key release highlights include:

  • CEL-based cluster selection and an Argo CD pull model add-on (1.0)
  • A gRPC-based hub-and-spoke connection, plus add-ons for Kueue MultiKueue and OpenTelemetry (1.1)
  • Advanced Placement configuration, automated hosting cluster resolution, and the introduction of the argocd-agent integration to provide highly scalable multi-cluster GitOps and complete application status visibility (1.2)
  • Enhancements to ManifestWork resource ordering and the graduation of the AddOnTemplate API to v1beta1 (1.3)
  • Syncing OCM PlacementDecisions to SIG Multicluster’s PlacementDecision API, ManifestWork observability, and security hardening such as network policies (1.4)

OCM works closely with the broader cloud native ecosystem. It implements and aligns with the Kubernetes SIG Multicluster APIs, supplies Argo CD with cluster decisions for GitOps deployments, and integrates with Cluster API for cluster lifecycle. KubeVela, KubeStellar, Kueue, and Meshery all document OCM integrations, and the project maintains add-ons and examples for Argo CD, Fluid, and OpenTelemetry. Twenty-seven maintainers from eight organizations, including Red Hat, Guidewire, eBay, AppsCode, and Spectro Cloud, lead the project.

OCM has demonstrated adoption across organizations including Alibaba Cloud, AppsCode, Guidewire, Red Hat, and Spectro Cloud. At eBay, OCM supports application deployment across more than 190 Kubernetes clusters through integrations with Argo CD. Groww uses OCM to support progressive application rollouts, while VESSEL AI leverages the project to manage GPU clusters and distribute AI workloads across cloud environments.

“As Kubernetes adoption expands across increasingly complex environments, organizations need open, interoperable approaches to managing clusters at scale,” said Karena Angell, CNCF Technical Oversight Committee member. “Open Cluster Management has demonstrated technical maturity, a growing contributor community, and meaningful adoption across the cloud native ecosystem. Its advancement to incubation reflects the project’s progress in helping organizations manage multicluster environments without relying on proprietary solutions.”

Main Components

Open Cluster Management’s main components consist of the following:

  • Cluster Manager: The hub side control plane that coordinates registration, work, placement, and add-ons.
  • Klusterlet: The agent on each managed cluster that registers it with the hub and applies instructions from it.
  • Cluster Inventory (registration): Registers manage clusters through a double opt-in handshake and mTLS connection, with certificate rotation and a dedicated namespace per cluster on the hub.
  • ManifestWork API: Distributes Kubernetes resources to managed clusters, with update strategies, conflict resolution, and status feedback. Agents pull work from the hub, so the hub does not store managed cluster credentials.
  • Placement API: Dynamically selects clusters using labels, resource capacity, or custom criteria and publishes the result as a PlacementDecision that any scheduler or controller can consume.
  • Add-on framework: A structure for projects to become multicluster aware, handling registration, lifecycle, configuration, and status reporting.
  • clusteradm: A command line tool to bootstrap a hub and join clusters.
  • Built-in extensions: Cluster API integration for cluster lifecycle, an Argo CD add-on for pull-based application delivery, and governance, risk, and compliance policy controllers.

Notable Milestones

  • 1,100 GitHub Stars
  • 1,370 pull requests 
  • 537 contributors from 84 organizations across 16 countries
CNCF-Hosted Projects

The CNCF Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) provides technical leadership to CNCF projects, overseeing their progression through maturity levels and supporting long-term sustainability. Projects advancing to incubation demonstrate growing adoption, technical maturity, and community development.

items.title: CNCF and SlashData Report Finds Cloud Native Developers Are More AI-Ready, Global Population Surpasses 21 Million
items.summary: New research released finds 75% of cloud native developers use AI coding tools, compared to 55% of non-cloud native developer peers Key Highlights: CNCF and SlashData released the State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. The report notes that the global cloud native developer population reached an estimated 21.2 million, representing approximately 41% of developers worldwide. Cloud native developers are significantly more likely to use AI coding tools than their non-cloud native counterparts (75% vs. 55%) and integrate AI into their services (67% vs. 38%), reinforcing the relationship between cloud native maturity and AI adoption. The report finds North America is now home to approximately 4 million cloud native developers. SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today released new findings from its State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report , developed in collaboration with SlashData . As AI adoption accelerates, the report findings highlight the growing relationship between cloud native infrastructure, platform engineering and the development of production-ready AI and agentic systems. “Cloud native is foundational to how the industry builds and operates modern software, and AI is accelerating that evolution,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “This report reinforces how cloud native technologies are supporting AI workloads. As organizations move to scale AI workloads, the need for reliable, scalable and observable infrastructure will grow. Open source technologies like Kubernetes and OpenTelemetry are helping provide the foundation for that transition.” Cloud native developers lead AI adoption as agentic systems move toward production As AI becomes deeply integrated into software development, the report finds that cloud native developers are significantly more likely to adopt AI tools and integrate AI capabilities into their applications. However, the distinction is less about how developers use AI and more about whether they adopt it in the first place. 75% of cloud native developers use AI coding tools , compared to 55% of non-cloud native developers. 67% of cloud native developers are integrating AI into their services , compared to 38% of non-cloud native developers. 49% of developers integrating AI into their services report having agentic systems in production , including internal and external-facing applications. 55% of developers building agentic services are cloud native , while the remaining 45% demonstrate that developers can integrate agentic capabilities without directly managing cloud native infrastructure. These findings suggest that cloud native developers are embracing AI while maintaining established engineering practices around oversight, reliability and control. In North America, this preference for supervised AI development is pronounced. Among cloud native developers in the region, 21% use AI to draft code before reviewing and editing it themselves, while just 12% report using autonomous agents for coding tasks. “Our research shows that cloud native maturity is becoming an important indicator of how actively developers engage with AI,” said Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData. “Cloud native developers are more likely to adopt AI tools and integrate AI into their services, but once developers begin using these technologies, their approaches are remarkably similar. This highlights the importance of cloud native infrastructure in supporting AI at scale, even when the developers building AI-powered applications aren’t directly interacting with the underlying infrastructure.” Global cloud native developer community surpasses 21 million The report estimates that the global cloud native developer population reached 21.2 million in Q3 2026, up from 15.6 million in Q3 2025 and 19.9 million in Q1 2026. Cloud native developers now account for approximately 41% of the global developer population, reflecting the continued expansion of cloud native technologies beyond traditional backend infrastructure and into a wider range of development disciplines. Key findings include: 21.2 million developers worldwide are cloud native , marking the first time the population has surpassed 20 million. North America is home to approximately 4 million cloud native developers , reinforcing the region’s vital role in the global cloud native ecosystem. More than 80% of professional backend services and web backend developers engage in cloud native practices and approaches. Approximately 7.5 million AI developers are cloud native , underscoring the growing intersection between AI development and cloud native technologies. While the pace of cloud native developer growth has moderated over the past six months, the report suggests that increased adoption of managed services and internal developer platforms may be making underlying cloud native technologies less visible to developers. As organizations standardize their infrastructure, developers may rely on Kubernetes and other cloud native technologies without directly interacting with or identifying the underlying platforms. Platform engineering becomes standard as AI infrastructure matures Platform engineering and DevOps standardization continue to reshape how organizations build, deploy and manage applications. The report finds that 93% of developers now work at organizations using some form of DevOps standardization or internal developer platform, up from 77% in Q3 2025. This shift reflects the growing maturity of cloud native infrastructure as organizations centralize tooling, improve developer productivity and streamline operations. At the same time, greater abstraction can make the underlying infrastructure less visible to developers, even as its importance to production applications increases. The report also examines the adoption of infrastructure technologies among backend developers: 40% use API gateways , making them the most widely adopted technology surveyed. 30% use microservices , reflecting their continued importance in modern application architectures. 21% use observability tools , highlighting the role of visibility into complex systems. 19% report using Kubernetes , although platform abstraction may contribute to underreporting of underlying infrastructure technologies. 8% use immutable infrastructure practices and 7% use chaos engineering , suggesting continued opportunities for advanced infrastructure practices to mature. As AI workloads grow in complexity, these underlying capabilities are highly relevant to production environments. AI inference and agentic systems introduce new demands around compute scheduling, resource efficiency, observability and reliable distributed operations, areas where cloud native technologies already provide established approaches. The report also identifies cost, data privacy and security as leading concerns among developers who have not yet integrated AI functionality into their services. As a result, infrastructure capable of supporting reliable operations, cost management and scalability will likely become more important. The findings reinforce cloud native’s expanding role in the AI ecosystem, not only for developers building and operating infrastructure directly, but also for the growing number of developers consuming managed AI services built on cloud native foundations.   • The report notes that the global cloud native developer population reached an estimated 21.2 million, representing approximately 41% of developers worldwide.

SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today released new findings from its State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, developed in collaboration with SlashData. As AI adoption accelerates, the report findings highlight the growing relationship between cloud native infrastructure, platform engineering and the development of production-ready AI and agentic systems.

“Cloud native is foundational to how the industry builds and operates modern software, and AI is accelerating that evolution,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “This report reinforces how cloud native technologies are supporting AI workloads. As organizations move to scale AI workloads, the need for reliable, scalable and observable infrastructure will grow. Open source technologies like Kubernetes and OpenTelemetry are helping provide the foundation for that transition.”

Cloud native developers lead AI adoption as agentic systems move toward production

As AI becomes deeply integrated into software development, the report finds that cloud native developers are significantly more likely to adopt AI tools and integrate AI capabilities into their applications. However, the distinction is less about how developers use AI and more about whether they adopt it in the first place.

  • 75% of cloud native developers use AI coding tools, compared to 55% of non-cloud native developers.
  • 67% of cloud native developers are integrating AI into their services, compared to 38% of non-cloud native developers.
  • 49% of developers integrating AI into their services report having agentic systems in production, including internal and external-facing applications.
  • 55% of developers building agentic services are cloud native, while the remaining 45% demonstrate that developers can integrate agentic capabilities without directly managing cloud native infrastructure.

These findings suggest that cloud native developers are embracing AI while maintaining established engineering practices around oversight, reliability and control.

In North America, this preference for supervised AI development is pronounced. Among cloud native developers in the region, 21% use AI to draft code before reviewing and editing it themselves, while just 12% report using autonomous agents for coding tasks.

“Our research shows that cloud native maturity is becoming an important indicator of how actively developers engage with AI,” said Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData. “Cloud native developers are more likely to adopt AI tools and integrate AI into their services, but once developers begin using these technologies, their approaches are remarkably similar. This highlights the importance of cloud native infrastructure in supporting AI at scale, even when the developers building AI-powered applications aren’t directly interacting with the underlying infrastructure.”

Global cloud native developer community surpasses 21 million

The report estimates that the global cloud native developer population reached 21.2 million in Q3 2026, up from 15.6 million in Q3 2025 and 19.9 million in Q1 2026. Cloud native developers now account for approximately 41% of the global developer population, reflecting the continued expansion of cloud native technologies beyond traditional backend infrastructure and into a wider range of development disciplines.

Key findings include:

  • 21.2 million developers worldwide are cloud native, marking the first time the population has surpassed 20 million.
  • North America is home to approximately 4 million cloud native developers, reinforcing the region’s vital role in the global cloud native ecosystem.
  • More than 80% of professional backend services and web backend developers engage in cloud native practices and approaches.
  • Approximately 7.5 million AI developers are cloud native, underscoring the growing intersection between AI development and cloud native technologies.

While the pace of cloud native developer growth has moderated over the past six months, the report suggests that increased adoption of managed services and internal developer platforms may be making underlying cloud native technologies less visible to developers. As organizations standardize their infrastructure, developers may rely on Kubernetes and other cloud native technologies without directly interacting with or identifying the underlying platforms.

Platform engineering becomes standard as AI infrastructure matures

Platform engineering and DevOps standardization continue to reshape how organizations build, deploy and manage applications. The report finds that 93% of developers now work at organizations using some form of DevOps standardization or internal developer platform, up from 77% in Q3 2025.

This shift reflects the growing maturity of cloud native infrastructure as organizations centralize tooling, improve developer productivity and streamline operations. At the same time, greater abstraction can make the underlying infrastructure less visible to developers, even as its importance to production applications increases.

The report also examines the adoption of infrastructure technologies among backend developers:

  • 40% use API gateways, making them the most widely adopted technology surveyed.
  • 30% use microservices, reflecting their continued importance in modern application architectures.
  • 21% use observability tools, highlighting the role of visibility into complex systems.
  • 19% report using Kubernetes, although platform abstraction may contribute to underreporting of underlying infrastructure technologies.
  • 8% use immutable infrastructure practices and 7% use chaos engineering, suggesting continued opportunities for advanced infrastructure practices to mature.

As AI workloads grow in complexity, these underlying capabilities are highly relevant to production environments. AI inference and agentic systems introduce new demands around compute scheduling, resource efficiency, observability and reliable distributed operations, areas where cloud native technologies already provide established approaches.

The report also identifies cost, data privacy and security as leading concerns among developers who have not yet integrated AI functionality into their services. As a result, infrastructure capable of supporting reliable operations, cost management and scalability will likely become more important.

The findings reinforce cloud native’s expanding role in the AI ecosystem, not only for developers building and operating infrastructure directly, but also for the growing number of developers consuming managed AI services built on cloud native foundations.

items.title: Donating KubeRay to CNCF
items.summary: The PARK stack (PyTorch, AI models, Ray, and Kubernetes) is emerging as the de facto open source standard for production AI. Within that stack, KubeRay has become the bridge connecting scalable AI applications built on Ray with the compute orchestration of Kubernetes. Nearly every core piece of the PARK stack already lives under the Linux Foundation: PyTorch and Ray through the PyTorch Foundation, and Kubernetes through the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). KubeRay was the missing piece. Today, we’re announcing that KubeRay is joining the CNCF, bringing the entire PARK stack under Linux Foundation governance and giving teams full confidence in its neutrality and openness. Scaling Ray clusters on Kubernetes KubeRay is a powerful, open source toolkit and Kubernetes operator designed to run distributed AI, machine learning, and Python workloads powered by Ray seamlessly on cloud-native infrastructure. As distributed AI workloads become a core cloud native construct, KubeRay bridges the gap between Python-first AI frameworks and Kubernetes-native infrastructure. KubeRay provides three Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for scaling and operating Ray workloads in production: RayCluster: The foundational building block for running Ray on Kubernetes. `RayCluster` manages the full lifecycle of a Ray cluster, automating head and worker pod provisioning, health checks, Global Control Service (GCS) fault tolerance, and dynamic autoscaling in coordination with the Ray Autoscaler. RayJob: Purpose-built for batch processing, distributed training, and reinforcement learning (RL) workloads. `RayJob` automatically provisions an ephemeral `RayCluster`, submits a Ray job once the cluster is ready, and tears down the cluster upon completion to maximize compute and accelerator utilization. RayService: Designed for long-lived, high-availability online inference with Ray Serve. `RayService` manages both the underlying `RayCluster` and the Ray Serve deployment graph, enabling zero-downtime rolling upgrades, automated failover, and seamless traffic routing for production AI services. Together, these custom resources provide the foundation for enterprises to build modern machine learning platforms on top of Ray and Kubernetes. For example, end users like Spotify use KubeRay to scale their internal machine learning platform, Hendrix, which is used to train and fine-tune Spotify’s machine learning models using Ray on GKE. “Running multimodal AI workloads at scale requires a platform with tight integration between Python-first AI and Kubernetes. KubeRay is that bridge, helping us scale reliably and manage complex agentic workflows At Hark, that is why we use it, and why I contribute: I want to help more builders scale production AI with confidence.” Kai-Hsun Chen, AI Infrastructure Lead, Hark Growing the KubeRay ecosystem Beyond core cluster lifecycle management, KubeRay has seen widespread adoption because of how deeply it integrates with other CNCF projects and the broader cloud-native ecosystem. Rather than reinventing infrastructure primitives, KubeRay plugs directly into the tools platform teams already rely on: Observability with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Fluent Bit: Ray uses OpenTelemetry within its metrics pipeline and exposes metrics in Prometheus format, enabling platform teams running KubeRay to monitor cluster utilization, task execution, and Ray Serve latency alongside their existing Kubernetes infrastructure. Paired with Fluent Bit for lightweight log collection and forwarding, operators can easily aggregate distributed worker and job logs across ephemeral and long-lived Ray clusters. Batch Scheduling and Quota Management with Kueue, Volcano, and KAI: As organizations scale distributed training across scarce GPU and TPU resources, KubeRay integrates natively with different schedulers to bring Kubernetes-native job queueing to `RayJob` and `RayCluster`. This enables gang scheduling (all-or-nothing pod placement), multi-tenant resource quotas, priority preemption, and topology-aware scheduling. Workload Security and Isolation: As AI workloads scale, robust security and multi-tenancy are critical. KubeRay provides the foundation to secure Ray clusters using automated mTLS and Kubernetes network policies. What’s Next? KubeRay’s success so far has been due to its fast-growing community members — we want to give thanks to everyone who has contributed to KubeRay so far. Becoming a CNCF sandbox project is just the beginning of KubeRay’s next chapter under open, vendor-neutral governance, and we’d love for you to be part of it. If you’re at KubeCon NA 2026, come meet the KubeRay maintainers at our Birds of a Feather (BoF) session to discuss the roadmap, share production use cases, and help shape the future of Ray on Kubernetes. Hark will also be giving a talk about how they use KubeRay for multimodal AI use cases as well. You can also connect with the community in the #kuberay channel on the CNCF or Ray Slack workspaces and attend our biweekly community meetings .

KubeRay provides three Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for scaling and operating Ray workloads in production:

  • RayCluster: The foundational building block for running Ray on Kubernetes. `RayCluster` manages the full lifecycle of a Ray cluster, automating head and worker pod provisioning, health checks, Global Control Service (GCS) fault tolerance, and dynamic autoscaling in coordination with the Ray Autoscaler.
  • RayJob: Purpose-built for batch processing, distributed training, and reinforcement learning (RL) workloads. `RayJob` automatically provisions an ephemeral `RayCluster`, submits a Ray job once the cluster is ready, and tears down the cluster upon completion to maximize compute and accelerator utilization.
  • RayService: Designed for long-lived, high-availability online inference with Ray Serve. `RayService` manages both the underlying `RayCluster` and the Ray Serve deployment graph, enabling zero-downtime rolling upgrades, automated failover, and seamless traffic routing for production AI services.

Together, these custom resources provide the foundation for enterprises to build modern machine learning platforms on top of Ray and Kubernetes. For example, end users like Spotify use KubeRay to scale their internal machine learning platform, Hendrix, which is used to train and fine-tune Spotify’s machine learning models using Ray on GKE.

“Running multimodal AI workloads at scale requires a platform with tight integration between Python-first AI and Kubernetes. KubeRay is that bridge, helping us scale reliably and manage complex agentic workflows At Hark, that is why we use it, and why I contribute: I want to help more builders scale production AI with confidence.”

Kai-Hsun Chen, AI Infrastructure Lead, Hark

Growing the KubeRay ecosystem

Beyond core cluster lifecycle management, KubeRay has seen widespread adoption because of how deeply it integrates with other CNCF projects and the broader cloud-native ecosystem. Rather than reinventing infrastructure primitives, KubeRay plugs directly into the tools platform teams already rely on:

  • Observability with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Fluent Bit: Ray uses OpenTelemetry within its metrics pipeline and exposes metrics in Prometheus format, enabling platform teams running KubeRay to monitor cluster utilization, task execution, and Ray Serve latency alongside their existing Kubernetes infrastructure. Paired with Fluent Bit for lightweight log collection and forwarding, operators can easily aggregate distributed worker and job logs across ephemeral and long-lived Ray clusters.
  • Batch Scheduling and Quota Management with Kueue, Volcano, and KAI: As organizations scale distributed training across scarce GPU and TPU resources, KubeRay integrates natively with different schedulers to bring Kubernetes-native job queueing to `RayJob` and `RayCluster`. This enables gang scheduling (all-or-nothing pod placement), multi-tenant resource quotas, priority preemption, and topology-aware scheduling.
  • Workload Security and Isolation: As AI workloads scale, robust security and multi-tenancy are critical. KubeRay provides the foundation to secure Ray clusters using automated mTLS and Kubernetes network policies.
What’s Next?

KubeRay’s success so far has been due to its fast-growing community members — we want to give thanks to everyone who has contributed to KubeRay so far.

Becoming a CNCF sandbox project is just the beginning of KubeRay’s next chapter under open, vendor-neutral governance, and we’d love for you to be part of it. 

If you’re at KubeCon NA 2026, come meet the KubeRay maintainers at our Birds of a Feather (BoF) session to discuss the roadmap, share production use cases, and help shape the future of Ray on Kubernetes. Hark will also be giving a talk about how they use KubeRay for multimodal AI use cases as well.

You can also connect with the community in the #kuberay channel on the CNCF or Ray Slack workspaces and attend our biweekly community meetings.

items.title: CNCF Hits Major Milestones with Global Community Growth, Record Industry Investment and a New Generation of Projects to Build AI Systems in Production
items.summary: New Sandbox projects, including Agent Substrate and OpenShell, expand CNCF’s portfolio to 231 projects as the community adds over 5.5 million cloud native developers in 12 months, welcomes eight Platinum memberships and brings together 82,000 attendees at events worldwide SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 – Nov. 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today highlighted a year of significant momentum, marked by new sandbox projects — including OpenShell and Agent Substrate — and milestones expanding open infrastructure for training AI models, scaling inference and securely operating autonomous agents. The announcement builds on continued member investment, a global cloud native developer population surpassing 21 million and technical progress across a foundation now spanning 231 projects. In the past year, cloud native and CNCF events brought together 82,000 attendees globally at record-breaking events across more than 50 countries, while 32 new projects expanded the foundation’s technology portfolio, including exciting new Sandbox Projects Agent Substrate and llm-d , as well as OpenShell secure runtimes for AI agents. That momentum extended with new Platinum members Adyen, Broadcom, CoreWeave, CVS, HAProxy, NVIDIA, OVHcloud and Vultr representing the chipmakers, neoclouds and enterprise users underpinning the next generation of AI infrastructure. “AI teams need control over where their models run, what their agents can do, and how their systems behave in production,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF. “A year ago, we were talking about the opportunity in inference. Today, this community is building the infrastructure to train models, run inference and put agents to work with the security and scale production demands. We’re bringing that work together in the open so developers retain choice across models, hardware and providers. Bring your hardest problems, contribute what you’ve learned and help us build what comes next.” OpenShell Brings Agent Runtime Security into Ecosystem Stewardship OpenShell is joining CNCF as a Sandbox project, bringing the secure runtime for autonomous AI agents into vendor-neutral, ecosystem-led stewardship. Spearheaded by NVIDIA, OpenShell governs how agents execute, which resources and data they can access and where inference requests are routed. It provides policy enforcement in the infrastructure surrounding an agent, helping organizations control access to files, networks, credentials and model endpoints as agents perform increasingly complex tasks and work at scale. The contribution gives developers, platform teams and security practitioners a direct role in shaping the runtime foundation for AI and addresses the security, control and governance challenges that stand between experimentation and production. An Expanding Foundation to Train, Infer and Act CNCF project contributions announced today broaden the technologies available to organizations building AI infrastructure: Agent Substrate provides a zero-trust runtime for executing AI agents on Kubernetes while isolating untrusted code. gVisor strengthens workload isolation through a user-space kernel that limits exposure to the host operating system. KubeRay supports running and managing Ray workloads on Kubernetes for distributed computing, including AI training and inference. OpenRL brings Kubernetes-native orchestration to reinforcement learning, helping teams coordinate the compute required for model post-training. OpenShell adds runtime governance and policy enforcement for autonomous agents. These projects build on substantial AI progress over the last twelve months: Distributed inference: llm-d joined CNCF and reached its 1.0 release, advancing an open framework for deploying and scaling distributed large language model inference. AI lifecycle maturity: Kubeflow graduated, recognizing the maturity of its ecosystem for data processing, model training, fine-tuning and serving. Accelerator efficiency: HAMi advanced to incubation, supporting the sharing and scheduling of heterogeneous accelerators on Kubernetes. Infrastructure capabilities: Kubernetes advanced workload-aware scheduling and Dynamic Resource Allocation, improving how complex AI workloads coordinate, compute and access specialized hardware. Interoperability: The Kubernetes AI Conformance Program reached 40 certified platforms driving community-led requirements for consistent AI infrastructure. Across the wider portfolio, Cloud Native Buildpacks , Karmada , Kubeflow , KubeVirt , NATS and OpenTelemetry also reached graduation, while CloudNativePG , K8gb , Meshery , and Open Cluster Management advanced to incubation. Together, these milestones strengthen the application delivery, orchestration, messaging, data and operational infrastructure on which production systems depend. A Global Community Building What Comes Next In 2026, the global cloud native developer community reached 21.2 million , while cloud native and CNCF events brought together 82,000 attendees across more than 50 countries. KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe set a new CNCF attendance record with nearly 13,500 attendees , alongside Kubernetes Community Days, meetups and specialized gatherings connecting practitioners worldwide. That growth is expanding the community’s reach and shared expertise. CNCF welcomed 58 new Ambassadors and added 28 Cloud Native Community Groups, creating more opportunities for local participation. Community members also published 40 new cloud native case studies and 12 reference architectures , turning production experience into practical guidance others can build on. Build the Future of Cloud and AI “The people who built Kubernetes are now working side by side with a new wave of contributors focused on inference, training and agents, and you can see it in our project and contributor growth,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of CNCF. “AI workloads are landing on cloud native infrastructure and the patterns for scaling them are being defined in CNCF projects right now. If you’re a developer who wants to shape how AI runs in production, this is the moment to get involved.” Looking ahead, CNCF also plans to introduce two additional AI focused certifications in 2027: Kubernetes AI Associate (KAIA) and Certified Kubernetes Inference Engineer (CKIE) . These upcoming credentials will further expand CNCF’s training and certification portfolio as AI and cloud native technologies continue to converge. CNCF invites developers, end users and technology providers to build the next era of cloud and AI: contribute code, share production experience, join community groups and invest in the projects global organizations depend on. The challenges of running AI in production are already here. Bring your toughest problems – and your expertise – to the community building the solutions. items.summary: New certification validates specialized expertise in Kubernetes networking, security and troubleshooting as demand for cloud native skills grows Key Highlights The Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE) joins CNCF’s certification portfolio, validating hands-on expertise in designing, securing and troubleshooting networking across production Kubernetes environments. CKNE certification and CKNE Certification Pathway (5 modules) reinforce CNCF’s commitment to accessible, vendor-neutral education helping individuals advance their careers while enabling organizations to build and maintain secure, reliable and scalable systems. CNCF to expand its certification roadmap with two additional credentials planned for 2027: Kubernetes AI Associate (KAIA) and Certified Kubernetes Inference Engineer (CKIE). SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation ® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced the global availability of the Certified Kubernetes Network Engineer (CKNE) certification. Developed in collaboration with Linux Foundation Education , the new exam is designed to validate hands-on expertise in designing, securing and troubleshooting networking across production Kubernetes environments. As organizations rely on Kubernetes to support all types of workloads including AI, networking has become a critical component of secure, reliable and scalable infrastructure. Developed in collaboration with Linux Foundation Education, the new exam is designed to validate hands-on expertise in designing, securing and troubleshooting networking across production Kubernetes environments. 

As organizations rely on Kubernetes to support all types of workloads including AI, networking has become a critical component of secure, reliable and scalable infrastructure. items.title: Researcher bypassed Meta smart glasses’ safeguards to run her own code
items.summary: We’ve written before about what Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses can see and hear , and who might get to use that information. Those worries focus on how the glasses handle information during normal use. A security researcher has now shown how to bypass a safeguard meant to stop unauthorized software running on them. Vulnerability researcher Paula, known online as pamoutaf, found a way to run her own software on a pair of Ray-Ban Meta glasses. For the technical details I’ll gladly refer you to her own post about it. The glasses are controlled by the Meta AI app on the owner’s phone. Developers can add their own apps to the glasses through a developer tool, and the phone sends that software to the glasses to install. The glasses were supposed to check that the software really came from Meta. In older firmware (up to and including version 126), they didn’t check, so the researcher could swap in an app of her own. Meta introduced a check in firmware version 127 to verify the app’s digital signature to prove that it came from Meta . The researcher found the on/off switch for that signature check came from a settings file passed along by the phone. The glasses only checked the file was correctly formed, not whether it had been tampered with. Changing a single byte in the file turned the signature check off. Once her app was running, she could send commands to the glasses from the paired phone over a wireless connection. The glasses have a camera, microphones and a wireless connection, and they sit on your face all day. A wearable that can be made to run unapproved code goes beyond a privacy-policy question. It becomes a security question about who controls the device. As we’ve seen, some cheaper smart glasses already are a security disaster . In this case the person running the code would be the person that controls the phone. If malicious software running on the glasses could access the camera or stored recordings, it could potentially send footage to an attacker’s server. Pamoutaf’s research doesn’t demonstrate that scenario, but it raises questions about what that software might be able to access. In her post she promised a follow-up exploring other potential ways to attack the glasses. How to stay safe Keep the glasses’ firmware and the Meta AI app updated, and avoid unofficial apps or modifications. If smart glasses are just another gadget to you, I’d leave them on the shelf. items.summary: Use the XQL query APIs. Start a query with /public_api/v1/xql/start_xql_query, which returns an execution ID. Fetch the results with /public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results in JSON. That call returns up to 1,000 results inline; anything bigger comes back as a stream ID you pass to /public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results_stream. Authentication uses two headers: your API key in Authorization and its ID in x-xdr-auth-id. Cortex XDR collects detailed endpoint telemetry, plus network and identity data in many deployments. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key. Create one in the Cortex XDR settings (the standard key type is simplest) with a role that can run XQL queries. Note the key and its ID. Your API URL. It’s shown when you create the key, in the form https://api- .xdr. .paloaltonetworks.com. License and quota. The XQL APIs need a Cortex XDR Pro license. Queries draw on your XQL quota, and you can run up to four API queries in parallel. The dataset. Endpoint telemetry is in xdr_data, with fields such as agent_hostname, event_type, action_process_image_command_line and actor_process_image_name. Build the query in the Query Builder first. Export with the XQL APIs XDR="https://api- .xdr. .paloaltonetworks.com" H1="Authorization: $XDR_API_KEY" H2="x-xdr-auth-id: $XDR_API_KEY_ID" # 1. start the query (timeframe in epoch milliseconds) QID=$(curl -sS -X POST "$XDR/public_api/v1/xql/start_xql_query" -H "$H1" -H "$H2" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"request_data": {"query": "dataset = xdr_data | filter agent_hostname = \"WS-042\" | fields _time, agent_hostname, event_type, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line, actor_process_image_name", "timeframe": {"from": 1792368000000, "to": 1792454400000}}}' \ | jq -r '.reply') # 2. wait for the results while :; do RESP=$(curl -sS -X POST "$XDR/public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results" -H "$H1" -H "$H2" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"request_data\": {\"query_id\": \"$QID\", \"pending_flag\": true, \"format\": \"json\"}}") [ "$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.reply.status')" != "PENDING" ] && break sleep 5 done # 3. up to 1,000 results inline; more through the stream STREAM=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.reply.results.stream_id // empty') if [ -n "$STREAM" ]; then curl -sS -X POST "$XDR/public_api/v1/xql/get_query_results_stream" -H "$H1" -H "$H2" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{\"request_data\": {\"stream_id\": \"$STREAM\", \"is_gzip_compressed\": false}}" > xdr_ws042_1019.jsonl else echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.reply.results.data[]' > xdr_ws042_1019.jsonl fi The timeframe above is 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. Yes, through separate incident and alert APIs. For LogTotal, export the telemetry behind them. What about raw third-party logs? items.title: North Korean Hackers Target Drone Technology and Software Supply Chains in New Cyberespionage Campaigns
items.summary: North Korean hackers have renewed efforts to steal drone technology while expanding attacks against software developers and the projects they maintain. Activity tracked between April and September 2026 shows Lazarus returning to European defense targets, while DeceptiveDevelopment used stolen developer credentials to spread malicious code through software supply chains. The campaigns share a familiar starting point: a convincing job offer that persuades someone to run attacker-controlled software. Their goals then diverge. Lazarus seeks access to sensitive defense systems and technical knowledge, while DeceptiveDevelopment turns compromised developer accounts into distribution channels, exposing users who never interacted with the original fake recruiter. ESET researchers identified updated malware across these operations, including MortPusLoader, LightlessTeaR, OmniStealer, and DEV#POPPER RAT. Their latest APT Activity Report describes changes in delivery, persistence, and command infrastructure. The findings build on earlier European drone industry attacks , but the latest reporting shows renewed targeting and a broader software distribution risk. North Korean Hackers Target Drone Technology and Software Supply Chains Operation DreamJob resumed targeting drone technology and related supply chains around June 2026, following a quiet period after activity documented in October 2025. items.title: How to Export Cortex XSIAM Logs
items.summary: Cortex XSIAM uses the same XQL query APIs as Cortex XDR: start a query, wait for results, and use a stream for anything over 1,000 rows. What’s different is the data. Third-party logs land in raw datasets, usually named _ _raw, and the original log line sits in the _raw_log field. Select that field, and the export gives you back exactly what the source sent. XSIAM is Palo Alto Networks’ SOC platform, and it’s where many former QRadar SaaS customers ended up after the 2024 deal. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key and URL. Create a key with a role that can run XQL queries; note the key, its ID and the API URL shown with it. Find the dataset. In the Query Builder, list datasets (dataset = offers suggestions). Raw third-party data follows the _ _raw pattern, for example fortinet_fortigate_raw. Endpoint telemetry is in xdr_data. Hot and cold storage. Recent data is in hot storage and queries quickly. Older data may be in cold storage, which needs its own query approach and costs more quota. Export with the XQL APIs To get raw lines from a FortiGate dataset: dataset = fortinet_fortigate_raw | filter _raw_log contains "web-03" | fields _time, _raw_log Run it through start_xql_query and get_query_results (plus get_query_results_stream above 1,000 rows), as in the Cortex XDR guide. Then turn the JSON into raw lines: jq -r '._raw_log' xsiam_fortigate_1019.jsonl > xsiam_fortigate_1019.log For normalized data across sources, query the data model (XDM) instead. You get consistent field names, but not the original wording. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file: raw lines from _raw_log, or the JSON rows. Sanitize. Review. items.title: Set your intended architecture with your coding agent, skip the diagram
items.summary: SonarQube Cloud now lets you define your project's intended architecture by working directly with your coding agent through the SonarQube CLI or the SonarQube MCP Server . Explore your current architecture through your agent, while it proposes components and the allowed relationships for your intended architecture that you confirm before saving. Deviations then surface as maintainability issues in your existing workflow, catching architectural drift before it compounds. Architectural debt does not accumulate at the same rate as code-level debt. It compounds 2.8 times faster, because a single misplaced dependency or an improperly exposed component does not stay contained. It ripples through every module that touches it, making the whole system harder to change safely. AI coding agents make this problem more urgent, not less. An AI agent can generate functioning code at a speed no human team can match, but it does so without knowing about allowable components dependencies, or which boundaries exist to keep your system modular. The result is architectural drift: code that passes tests and does what was asked, while quietly violating the structure your team relies on to keep the codebase maintainable. Until now, fixing that gap meant building your intended architecture by hand, a process that most teams deprioritized because it competed with the time they needed to ship features. SonarQube Cloud closes that gap by putting the work where development already happens: inside a conversation with your coding agent. What does it mean to define architecture with a coding agent? Instead of opening a tool to document your architecture, you ask your coding agent questions about your codebase and let it do the analysis. Your agent reads the current architecture of your project directly from SonarQube Cloud through the SonarQube CLI or the SonarQube MCP Server, the same way it reads any other context about your code. You can ask it what you would ask a teammate who already knows the system: What are the top-level components of this project? How does the billing component use the persistence component? Which components depend on this component? Your agent starts with a focused view of the architecture and requests more detail on specific components as the conversation requires it, rather than loading the entire system at once. How do you turn current architecture into intended architecture? Exploring the current state is only half the job. You can ask your agent to help define how the project should be built going forward. Your agent proposes components and the relationships allowed between them, based on what it understands about your codebase from SonarQube. You decide what to keep and what to leave out of your intended architecture that it suggests. Before anything is saved, you can ask your agent to preview the changes, review them with you, and confirm them together. This matters for a practical reason: your agent works within your own SonarQube permissions. It can only change what you are authorized to change, so architectural authority stays with the people accountable for it, not with the agent itself. Where does the intended architecture live once it's defined? The result is stored as the intended architecture in SonarQube Cloud, structured the same way a model built through the web editor is. From that point forward, every analysis checks your code against it. If a software developer or an agent introduces a relationship that violates the intended architecture, such as an illegal dependency between components, SonarQube Cloud raises it as a maintainability issue in the same workflow your team already uses to triage other findings. You do not need a separate architecture review process. The deviation shows up where your team is already looking. You can keep refining the architecture with your agent or manually in the UI over time, one level of detail at a time, as the system evolves and new components are added. Can you automate architecture setup across many projects? For teams managing more than a handful of projects, manually repeating this process for every repository does not scale. The same capabilities used by your coding agent are available as public Web API endpoints, documented for building your own integrations. You can read the current architecture of a project or create, read, replace, and delete its intended architecture programmatically. That makes it possible to push a standardized intended architecture to many projects from a single template, or feed architecture data into internal tooling your team already relies on. Access follows the same governance model as the conversational workflow. Reading architecture data requires "Browse" permission on the project. Writing to it requires the "Administer architecture" permission, keeping that authority with the people responsible for setting the standard. Get started Install the SonarQube CLI and log in to SonarQube Cloud. If you use Claude Code or Cursor, run Sonar architecture install-skill in your terminal. This teaches your agent how to explore the architecture through a skill and how to confirm changes with you before saving. With other agents, ask them to run Sonar architecture --help to see the available commands. In your project, start a new agent session and ask "Show me the top-level architecture of this project," then "Help me define the intended architecture." If you use the SonarQube MCP Server instead, update to the latest release with architecture support, add architecture to your existing SONARQUBE_TOOLSETS configuration, and restart the SONARQUBE MCP SERVER connection. Architecture management with a coding agent is available now in SonarQube Cloud , with support for Java , C# , JavaScript , TypeScript , and Python .

items.title: Verification is the factory's feedback system
items.summary: Agents have made code abundant, but confidence is scarce, specifically confidence that the code is correct, secure, and ready to ship. Developers tell us that 5% of organizations run AI software factories today and 34% expect to within a year. As factories take on more of the work, the quality of what they ship will depend less on which model writes the code and more on how well each factory checks it. Teams have to engineer confidence into the software factory the same way they engineer reliability into any production system, and that work starts with verification. Benedikt Stemmildt, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of hackers&wizards and co-author with Alex Merced of Building the Agentic Software Factory , develops these systems with clients every day. On the latest episode of The Next Commit , he told host Tom Howlett that "ultimately this is all about trust." For Benedikt, building that trust means designing factories to run without a human in the loop and giving them checks the team can rely on in place of reading every change. Turn each failure into a check Teams improve a software factory by turning each failure into a new check that the factory applies to every change. In that sense, verification is the factory’s feedback system. Teams get the most from it when they run checks inside the development loops, starting with the agentic loop, so each check can shape a change while the agent is still writing it. Teams that build it in this way end up with clear intent, guardrails that keep agents on track, independent verification, and evidence that every check ran. A factory that falls short on any of those gives its owners little reason to trust what it ships. When Benedikt finds a problem in what a factory produced, he leaves the feature code alone and changes the factory. "I'm reviewing the artifact the factory produced," he says. "If I see something that isn't what we want, I fix the factory." He also starts clients on narrow, repeated work such as dependency updates, because the team already knows which verifications that lane needs before the factory runs. Confidence needs both kinds of verification Sonar embeds two kinds of verification at every stage. Deterministic verification is a repeatable assessment based on structural rules and known patterns, and it gives the same answer every time without changing that answer under pressure, which makes it a dependable gate for the standards a team has written down. Agentic verification applies deliberate, context-aware reasoning to verify intent and discover anomalies, covering business logic, deep semantics, and other problems no rule anticipates. Teams need both kinds, because each one checks what the other can't. Benedikt strikes the same balance in his factories, adding lint rules and ArchUnit tests "so that you can trust the non-determinism more" and handling contextual problems with skills and instructions. He warns that a factory loaded with too many hard constraints becomes "like a cage" that stalls or keeps pulling in a human, while a factory with too few gives its owners nothing to trust. Both kinds also have to run independently of the agent, model, or developer that wrote the code. Sonar verifies separately from the agents and models a team uses, so one standard holds across all of them, including code written by people. A factory that asks another model to judge its output inherits that model's inconsistency, and recent research shows frontier LLM judges change 7% to 17% of their verdicts when asked the same question again, even with their randomness setting turned all the way down. As Benedikt points out, teams trust senior engineers even though people are non-deterministic, because a senior engineer works within a known range and won't do anything wildly wrong. Agents carry no such guarantee, and he describes results that leave you asking "what on earth?" Teams need checks that stay the same no matter which agent made the change. One standard that teaches the agent in every loop A check that only reports a problem invites the agent to make the warning disappear, and Benedikt's linter example demonstrates the cost. A linter flags a 15-line method against a 10-line limit, and the agent "will just cut it in half," producing two shorter methods that pass the check and weaken the design. An experienced developer would read the warning as a reason to rethink the method's responsibilities, but that knowledge never appears in the message. Benedikt argues that most of our tooling was written for senior engineers, while agents benefit from explicit guidance the way junior developers do. Sonar issues include rule descriptions that explain why an issue matters and remediation guidance that points toward a sound correction, which gives an agent the context to fix the underlying problem rather than game the check. Sonar applies that standard wherever agents touch code. In the agentic loop, Sonar Vortex gives the agent context and constraints before it writes, verifies each change against the same SonarQube quality profile that gates merges, and prompts the agent to correct its output when a check fails. In the CI verification loop, SonarQube sets the standard through quality profiles and quality gates, and Gitar reviews each pull request for logic and intent and iterates on fixes until CI is green. SonarQube sets the standard; Gitar enforces it at merge speed. In the code maintenance loop, SonarQube Remediation Agent fixes issues in the background and rechecks each fix with the engine that found it, so only verified fixes ship. Every check leaves a consistent, auditable record, which helps a team understand a codebase it no longer reads line by line. Benedikt considers ownership of that standard the hardest part of building factories. "When we build factories with our clients, it's not a technology problem, not at all," he says. He describes the factory as an internal product, built by factory engineers and fed by product engineers who work closely with the business, and he notes that teams are still working out who owns context, skills, and verification between them. A shared verification standard gives both groups the same definition of good. Deciding what the factory treats as “good” The teams building software factories today will decide what their factories treat as “good.” Benedikt closed the episode with advice for developers adjusting to the change: "Find your new flow because this is not going away." Listen to the full episode of The Next Commit with Benedikt Stemmildt , then explore how Sonar's AI code verification fits into your software factory.

As Benedikt points out, teams trust senior engineers even though people are non-deterministic, because a senior engineer works within a known range and won't do anything wildly wrong. Agents carry no such guarantee, and he describes results that leave you asking "what on earth?" Teams need checks that stay the same no matter which agent made the change.

One standard that teaches the agent in every loop

A check that only reports a problem invites the agent to make the warning disappear, and Benedikt's linter example demonstrates the cost. A linter flags a 15-line method against a 10-line limit, and the agent "will just cut it in half," producing two shorter methods that pass the check and weaken the design. An experienced developer would read the warning as a reason to rethink the method's responsibilities, but that knowledge never appears in the message. Benedikt argues that most of our tooling was written for senior engineers, while agents benefit from explicit guidance the way junior developers do.

Sonar issues include rule descriptions that explain why an issue matters and remediation guidance that points toward a sound correction, which gives an agent the context to fix the underlying problem rather than game the check. Sonar applies that standard wherever agents touch code. In the agentic loop, Sonar Vortex gives the agent context and constraints before it writes, verifies each change against the same SonarQube quality profile that gates merges, and prompts the agent to correct its output when a check fails. In the CI verification loop, SonarQube sets the standard through quality profiles and quality gates, and Gitar reviews each pull request for logic and intent and iterates on fixes until CI is green. SonarQube sets the standard; Gitar enforces it at merge speed. In the code maintenance loop, SonarQube Remediation Agent fixes issues in the background and rechecks each fix with the engine that found it, so only verified fixes ship. Every check leaves a consistent, auditable record, which helps a team understand a codebase it no longer reads line by line.

Benedikt considers ownership of that standard the hardest part of building factories. "When we build factories with our clients, it's not a technology problem, not at all," he says. He describes the factory as an internal product, built by factory engineers and fed by product engineers who work closely with the business, and he notes that teams are still working out who owns context, skills, and verification between them. A shared verification standard gives both groups the same definition of good.

Deciding what the factory treats as “good”

The teams building software factories today will decide what their factories treat as “good.” Benedikt closed the episode with advice for developers adjusting to the change: "Find your new flow because this is not going away."

items.title: Portfolio Hierarchies arrives in SonarQube Cloud
items.summary: Enterprise organizations running dozens or hundreds of projects often manage their software projects as a hierarchical relationship. A hierarchy that exists only on paper is a hierarchy nobody can navigate, govern, or trust. This release gives that structure a visual, navigable interface. SonarQube Cloud now provides a dedicated portfolio hierarchy management in a UI that lets enterprise admins, divisional directors, and CISOs see parent-child portfolio relationships at a glance, understand exactly where they stand within a deep structure, and build or modify that structure with guardrails that prevent invalid changes before they happen. Who can use SonarQube Cloud portfolio hierarchy management? This release is built for enterprise teams managing multi-level portfolio structures across many projects and teams from a single interface. It is currently available to everyone with a SonarQube Cloud Enterprise plan. What's new in SonarQube Cloud enterprise portfolio management? Visual hierarchy at unlimited depth Organizational structures do not stop at two or three levels, so the hierarchy view does not either. The portfolio hierarchy management UI renders a full tree view of parent-child portfolio relationships, supporting unlimited nesting depth in this first version. Each level uses iconography and labeling to make the list easy to follow, no matter how many levels it has. Breadcrumb signposting at every level Losing track of your position inside a deep hierarchy is not a cosmetic inconvenience, it is a governance risk: a change made at the wrong level can misattribute metrics or break reporting for an entire division. A breadcrumb trail shows your current position in the structure at every level you navigate, so you always know exactly where a given portfolio sits relative to the rest of the organization before you act on it. Circular reference protection with plain-language messages A circular reference, a loop or self-link in the hierarchy, is not just an error state, it is a structural problem that can silently corrupt reporting if it goes undetected. SonarQube Cloud now prevents circular relationships in portfolio hierarchies, for example placing a parent portfolio under one of its own children. It blocks the change before saving and displays a plain-language message explaining why the relationship is not allowed. Guided link and unlink flows with confirmation Restructuring a portfolio hierarchy has real consequences for reporting and compliance, so making that change should never be a single accidental click. Linking a child portfolio to a parent, or unlinking one from the hierarchy, now runs through a guided flow with an explicit confirmation step before the change commits, giving admins a clear understanding of the consequences before they act. Clear level distinction at any depth Telling parent from child at a glance matters more as a hierarchy grows, not less. Each level in the tree is visually distinguished through indentation, iconography, and labeling. Therefore, the relationship between any two portfolios is clear, without requiring a user to manually trace the structure. Performance built for scale SonarQube Cloud’s portfolio hierarchy view lets users expand and collapse branches to explore nested portfolios, revealing child portfolios as branches are expanded, rather than displaying every level at once. Keyboard accessibility The hierarchy tree is fully keyboard-navigable, with appropriate ARIA roles applied to parent-child relationships, so the interface is usable for admins who rely on keyboard navigation rather than a mouse. How do I get started with portfolio hierarchy management in SonarQube Cloud? The portfolio hierarchy management feature is available now to eligible SonarQube Cloud Enterprise customers. A new portfolio hierarchy guide walks through building, navigating, and managing a hierarchy end to end, and the Enterprise admin documentation has been updated to reflect the new interface and workflows. Organizing structure is the first step. Governing it at scale is the reason that structure needs to be visible in the first place.
