items.title: Weird licenses and the new open source
items.summary: Somewhere on an IRC channel, I ended up in a conversation about the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License . It wasn't the first time weird licenses were discussed there: Reticulum 's sparked some interesting discussions as well. Let's start from the beginning. If you don't want to read the Wikipedia article on Free Software , a couple of years ago, I gave a small presentation at school as part of the "Oral communication in English" course, which is a (shoddy) cake-based explanation of the topic. Long story short, a Free Software is a software with 4 freedoms: The freedom to run the program as you wish, for any purpose. The freedom to study how the program works, and change it to make it do what you wish. Access to the source code is a precondition for this. The freedom to redistribute copies so you can help others. The freedom to distribute copies of your modified versions to others. By doing this you can give the whole community a chance to benefit from your changes. There is also the term Open Source, which is more or less Free Software but without the sociopolitical aspect of it, which is like a pizza without olives, or art without context: something devoid of meaning, a business-oriented product instead of a creation. Like in every sociopolitical endeavour, people sometimes disagree, leading to subtle but important variations. One of the most important one in the Free Software movement has been the question of the copyleft : should derivatives of Free Software be licensed under the same license? Some licenses, like the GPL says yes and this includes everything built on top of GPL code, the LGPL says that only code under LGPL needs to be released as LGPL, and others, called permissive licenses, like the BSD and MIT don't impose such restrictions. The Free Software movement started in 1986, so we're around 40 years later now, and the picture is pretty bleak: technically, one could argue that it won, as every computer-using company in the world depends on Free Software one way or the other: Firefox, Linux, VLC, Chrome, Ubuntu, Apache, nginx, Wikipedia, Open Street Map, Open Food Facts, … as well as more fundamental software components like curl, libxml, busybox, OpenSSL, GCC, clang, … Yet virtually none of them do contribute back to those commons, some of them being thanklessly maintained by a random person in Nebraska . Worse, a handful of computer-related companies ("cloud providers") are making ungodly amount of money renting infrastructure running Free Software, most smart™ devices are running Free Software, every single software producing/selling company depends on Free Software, and again, almost none contribute back meaningfully. A small number are trying to sponsor some projects they're depending on, but it often feels like a crass move for software that are maintained as a hobby: "Could you please garden a bit more efficiently, and add 150 apple trees to your small garden? We need it for our business, here is a 1000€ one-time payment" With AI making everything worse, Free Software maintainers are now wasting their time dealing with unreviewable useless pull-requests, drowning into a sea of low-quality no-fix-provided bug reports, being demoralized by vibe-coded forks adding shiny features that are never going to be upstreamable and thus upstreamed. It really feels as if nobody is even contemplating making the pedestrian effort of trying to avoid murdering the golden goose. Copyleft does help to mitigate those behaviours a bit, as companies aren't usually big fans to having to release their secret source code. The Asahi Linux project recently re-licensed its software from MIT to LGPL, to make it, if only symbolically, harder for people to profit from the labor without giving anything back. Unfortunately, there are a handful of tricks to bypass copyleft: don't use GPL as all, use strong boundaries (like Android is doing: Linux for its kernel, but everything running on top of it can have whatever license), rent the software to the users (every Cloud is doing that, and most ISP too), provide a context-free dump of the modifications and prevent users from modifying the code their devices are running, simplify ignore the license as the odds of somebody suing you are low, … If copyleft isn't the answer, maybe it's time to find better licenses? In my opinion, the freedom 0, being able to run the program for whatever purpose, might be the crux of the problem. Reticulum 's license has the following paragraph, because of course a decentralised secure communication network could help killing people more efficiently: The Software shall not be used in any kind of system which includes amongst its functions the ability to purposefully do harm to human beings. This sounds reasonable in theory, but it means that it's not Free anymore. Do we care? Well, Linux distributions usually have strict policies ( debian , fedora , …) when it comes to what software they package, with non-Free ones being either forbidden, on living in their own not-enabled-by-default dedicated repository. One step further is the The Filthy Human Hands (FHH) License , with: No part of a work under this license may be used or reproduced in any manner by organizations or businesses with more than fifty (50) employees. An exception is granted to allow ISPs and other hosting services to reproduce the work for the purposes of display and distribution. No part of a work under this license may be used or reproduced in any manner which promotes bigotry of any kind. This includes but is not limited to fascism, racism, sexism, misogyny, ableism, transphobia (including erasure and/or denial of nonbinary identities), homophobia, ageism, sane-ism (including denial of multiplicity and/or plurality), and discrimination against non-human identities. What's interesting here, from a technical point of view, is that this isn't really enforceable, legally speaking, as most terms are pretty vague. I think it's by design, and must be taken as a statement. One could use any other open-to-interpretation terms and obtain the same effects, namely that any entity with a legal department won't use it, and those small enough to not have one won't be able to sell/rent to those who do. What's beautiful about it, is that it does fit perfectly into the idea of the small web, of small communities with bespoke governance, of bricolage and of excluding authoritarianism/capitalism/morons/… by design. Given the current dire state of the world, I think it's time to realise that Free Software isn't enough, and that not wanting to have code ending up in whatever war machine bombing kids and families is less radical than the idea of Free Software at its inception 40 years ago. I'd love a weird-license repositories in Linux distributions with lovely, quirky, useful, useless, handcrafted software!

items.title: Critical Apache Airflow RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Execute Code Without Authentication
items.summary: Apache Airflow has a critical remote code execution flaw that lets anyone with write access to the Celery message broker run code on worker nodes. The attacker needs no credentials, DAG, or scheduler. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-68982 and is classified as CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function. It affects Airflow versions before 3.4.0 that run CeleryExecutor. Airflow gives a worker three ways to receive instructions. The web UI and REST API require credentials. ExecuteTask messages on the broker carry a signed JWT, and the Execution API validates it through supervise_task() before the task runs. ExecuteCallback messages use the same execute_workload Celery task and the same broker, but nothing validates them. The execute_workload task deserializes any JSON body into a typed object based only on its declared shape. There is no signature, no HMAC, and no broker-side ACL. In version 3.2.1, execute_callback_workload() reads the path and kwargs values from the message, calls import_module and getattr, and then runs the callable with the attacker’s arguments. In 3.3.0, this moved into a forked CallbackSubprocess. It builds an httpx. Client with the token but makes no network call and checks nothing, so the callback still runs first. Because import_module can reach any module in the worker’s environment, the attacker gets full code execution. A message that names os.system with a shell command is enough. Critical Apache Airflow RCE Flaw Researcher Or Sahar of Reflectiz confirmed this on Airflow 3.2.1 and 3.3.0 in Docker Compose labs with a Redis broker and a PostgreSQL backend. The callback path was built for Deadline Alerts, which run a function when a DAG run misses its deadline. The feature is still marked experimental, but that does not limit exposure. The execute_workload task and its ExecuteCallback handler register on every CeleryExecutor worker as soon as the Celery provider loads. A deployment does not have to use Deadline Alerts to be vulnerable. The attack also leaves no trace in Airflow. The proof of concept created zero DagRuns and zero TaskInstances, and /api/v2/dags still returned total_entries as 0. A recorded demo went further and dumped the worker’s hostname and every AIRFLOW__* environment variable, including the Fernet key. Apache rates the flaw as Important and has not published a CVSS score. Reflectiz scored it 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. Reflectiz also reported that 198 of 211 reachable Redis brokers in Airflow and Celery clusters answered without authentication. The flaw echoes CVE-2020-11981, an earlier case where broker access led to code execution on Airflow 1.10.10 and earlier. Airflow 3.4.0, released November 6, 2026, fixes the flaw. The worker now redeems a single-use token with the Execution API before any callback runs. Apply the upgrade to the Execution API server and every CeleryExecutor worker. No earlier patched release exists. Until the upgrade is done, turn on Redis AUTH or a RabbitMQ username and password, and block ports 6379 and 5672 from the internet. Since Airflow’s UI will not show this activity, audit broker traffic and Celery worker process logs for unexpected execute_workload messages. Exposed Redis servers are a common target. Cyber Security News covered how hackers turned more than 3,500 Redis servers into Monero miners , and also reported on Apache Airflow flaws that expose sensitive data . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How to Export LimaCharlie Logs
items.summary: Install the LimaCharlie CLI (pip install limacharlie), log in with your organization ID and an API key, and run an LCQL query with limacharlie search run for the time range you need, with JSON output. Events come back in LimaCharlie’s {routing, event} structure. For continuous, bulk export, configure an Output to S3, Google Cloud Storage or another destination. LimaCharlie keeps a year of telemetry in its Insight data lake by default, which makes after-the-fact investigation unusually practical. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key and your OID. Both are in the web app under Access Management → REST API . Give the key the permissions needed to query Insight. Queries cost money. LCQL queries are billed by the data they scan. Dry runs give you an estimate first. Narrow by platform, event type and host before you widen the time range. Know the event types. LimaCharlie names events by type: NEW_PROCESS, DNS_REQUEST, NETWORK_CONNECTIONS, WEL (Windows event logs) and so on. Pick the ones that matter for your question. Export with the CLI pip install limacharlie limacharlie auth login # asks for your OID and API key limacharlie search run \ --query 'plat == windows | NEW_PROCESS DNS_REQUEST | routing/hostname == "ws-042"' \ --start $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s) \ --end $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s) \ --oid --output json > lc_ws042_1019.json An LCQL query has parts separated by pipes: a sensor selector (plat == windows), the event types, a filter, and optionally a projection of fields. If the output is an array, flatten it with jq -c ‘.[]’. The CLI can also generate an LCQL query from a plain-language description (limacharlie ai generate-query), which helps when you don’t remember the field paths. Bulk: Outputs For ongoing export, add an Output in the web app that sends events (and detections or audit logs, if you want them) to S3, Google Cloud Storage, a SIEM or a webhook. Outputs send data from the moment they’re created. For history, query Insight as above. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Authentication errors Wrong OID or key, or missing permissions Recreate the key with query permissions Query is slow or expensive Too wide: all events, all sensors Add a sensor selector and event types No results Hostname in the wrong field, or wrong event type Check field paths with a small query first Nothing older than a year Insight retention Use your Output destination for older data FAQ Can LimaCharlie collect EVTX files from an endpoint? Yes, as artifacts collected from the sensor, and Windows event logs also stream in as WEL events. Is there an older interactive query mode? Yes. Install the LimaCharlie CLI (pip install limacharlie), log in with your organization ID and an API key, and run an LCQL query with limacharlie search run for the time range you need, with JSON output. Events come back in LimaCharlie’s {routing, event} structure. For continuous, bulk export, configure an Output to S3, Google Cloud Storage or another destination.

LimaCharlie keeps a year of telemetry in its Insight data lake by default, which makes after-the-fact investigation unusually practical. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get events out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

An API key and your OID. Both are in the web app under Access Management → REST API. Give the key the permissions needed to query Insight.

Queries cost money. LCQL queries are billed by the data they scan. Dry runs give you an estimate first. Narrow by platform, event type and host before you widen the time range.

Know the event types. LimaCharlie names events by type: NEW_PROCESS, DNS_REQUEST, NETWORK_CONNECTIONS, WEL (Windows event logs) and so on. Pick the ones that matter for your question.

Export with the CLI 
pip install limacharlie
limacharlie auth login        # asks for your OID and API key

limacharlie search run \
  --query 'plat == windows | NEW_PROCESS DNS_REQUEST | routing/hostname == "ws-042"' \
  --start $(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s) \
  --end $(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s) \
  --oid  --output json > lc_ws042_1019.json

An LCQL query has parts separated by pipes: a sensor selector (plat == windows), the event types, a filter, and optionally a projection of fields. If the output is an array, flatten it with jq -c ‘.[]’.

The CLI can also generate an LCQL query from a plain-language description (limacharlie ai generate-query), which helps when you don’t remember the field paths.

Bulk: Outputs

For ongoing export, add an Output in the web app that sends events (and detections or audit logs, if you want them) to S3, Google Cloud Storage, a SIEM or a webhook. Outputs send data from the moment they’re created. For history, query Insight as above.

  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review.

items.title: New Mirax Android Malware Uses Accessibility Services to Remotely Control Phones and Steal Bank Funds
items.summary: An Android banking malware campaign is using advertisements inside streaming apps to turn everyday phones into tools for financial theft. Mirax, the malware abuses Accessibility Services to watch screens, capture passwords, intercept verification codes, and let criminals operate banking apps directly on infected devices. Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers across the Middle East, Türkiye, and Africa were confirmed infected between March and September 2026. Reported fraud cases point to losses reaching millions of US dollars, although the confirmed figures cover only infections and transactions visible to investigators and affected banks. Researchers from Group-IB identified the campaign in a technical investigation published November 5, noting sharp increases in activity around Eid and late July. The operation remained active when the report appeared, with its operators changing application names and infrastructure to complicate detection. New Mirax Android Malware Uses Accessibility Services Evidence suggests the infection begins with advertisements or video links inside low-reputation streaming apps available through Google Play. Those links direct users to a separate installer outside the official store. Similar fake streaming app campaigns have used entertainment offers to persuade victims to install remote-control malware and approve dangerous permissions. One confirmed Mirax installer pretended to be “TikTok 18+,” an imitation unrelated to TikTok or ByteDance. It retrieved the second-stage payload, which disguised itself as Google Play Services. Its displayed name substituted a Cyrillic “о” for the Latin letter, making the fraudulent system component harder to distinguish at a glance. The crucial step is persuading victims to enable Accessibility access. Mirax actively guides users toward granting this permission rather than simply displaying a request. ‘Google Play Services’ Interface prompts displayed to targets leading to Accessibility Service authorization (Source – Group-IB) Once enabled, the malware can observe the interface and perform actions on the victim’s behalf, giving operators an interactive route into banking sessions. Mirax combines that access with keylogging, SMS interception, notification collection, and screen monitoring. It can capture a phone’s unlock PIN, password, or pattern and replay the stolen secret later. Operators can therefore unlock unattended devices, open banking apps, add beneficiaries, and initiate transfers while the owner is not watching. This makes the fraud difficult to separate from legitimate activity. Transactions originate from the customer’s actual phone and banking application, rather than an unfamiliar device. Earlier reporting on Mirax residential proxy capabilities also described how compromised phones can relay traffic, allowing attackers to use victims’ genuine internet addresses. Investigators documented international transfers and evidence suggesting mule accounts in India helped move stolen funds. However, tracing remained ongoing, and the report does not establish the final destination of every payment. Its loss estimate is a confirmed baseline, not a complete accounting of the campaign. items.title: CISA Confirms Hackers are Exploiting SSHole, the OpenSSH Vulnerability
items.summary: CISA has flagged active exploitation of SSHole, an OpenSSH authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123158) that lets remote attackers access certain Linux accounts without a valid password or SSH key. The OpenSSH flaw affects specific server configurations, carries a CVSS score of 8.1, and was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, with a November 12 remediation deadline. The entry requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 and lists ransomware use as unknown. Organizations should assess exposed systems and follow vendor guidance. SSHole affects OpenSSH on Linux when the server uses musl libc, a system software library, and checks passwords without PAM, the Linux authentication framework. Alpine Linux is one affected platform. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 need the upstream fix or a patched distribution package. As explained in Cybersecurity News’s earlier OpenSSH analysis , several conditions must exist together. Password authentication must be enabled, the target account’s stored password field must contain *, and another local account must hold a valid SHA-crypt password hash. Simply running an Alpine container does not establish exposure. The failure occurs when musl’s crypt() function receives an overly long password. For the affected hashing path, input exceeding 256 bytes can make the function return * as an error marker. OpenSSH may compare that marker with the target account’s stored * and accept the login. The documented trigger range is 257 to 1,024 bytes. Active Exploitation of OpenSSH SSHole Flaw Accounts with valid password hashes are not bypassed through this mechanism. The risk concerns accounts whose password fields contain the matching marker, even when administrators intended those accounts to use SSH keys. The official CVE record identifies the underlying problem as a password hash interpretation error. The supplied SANS Internet Storm Center findings describe deliberate attempts using passwords filled with repeated “A” characters. Researcher Johannes Ullrich recorded 232 long-password requests on November 5 and 713 on November 6. These totals represent suspicious requests, not confirmed breaches or separate attackers. Cowrie honeypots record only the first 255 password characters, limiting analysis of longer inputs. Ullrich suspected some logins succeeded, but the supplied account does not confirm successful sessions. CISA’s listing provides the broader exploitation warning. Administrators should install patched packages and restart sshd. OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains the upstream workaround, while distribution fixes may keep older version banners. Where updates must wait, setting PasswordAuthentication no blocks this path; confirm working key access before changing settings. Investigation should cover successful password logins to accounts without usable passwords, unexpected privilege changes, and newly added authorized keys. Earlier SSH honeypot research shows why monitoring must include non-interactive commands after login. Updating closes the flaw, but teams must also check whether attackers already used the affected account to run commands, change files, or establish continued access before the fix was applied. items.title: How to Export Amazon Security Lake Logs
items.summary: Amazon Security Lake stores your data in S3 as Parquet files in the OCSF schema, so you don’t download it directly. You query it. Use Amazon Athena with an UNLOAD statement and format = ‘JSON’: Athena writes the results as JSON lines to an S3 prefix you choose, and you download that. Security Lake tables live in a Glue database named amazon_security_lake_glue_db_ , one table per source. Security Lake centralizes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53, Security Hub findings, EKS audit logs and third-party sources in one normalized format. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Query access. Use the Security Lake delegated administrator account, or a subscriber with query access. Access is governed by Lake Formation, so you need SELECT on the tables, plus Athena permissions and write access to an S3 bucket for the export. Find the tables. In Athena, open the database for your region. Table names follow the pattern amazon_security_lake_table_ _ _ , for example amazon_security_lake_table_eu_west_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0. The region uses underscores. Partitions keep costs down. Tables are partitioned by region, accountid and eventday (YYYYMMDD). Athena bills by data scanned, so always filter on eventday. Export with Athena UNLOAD In the Athena console, or with aws athena start-query-execution: UNLOAD ( SELECT * FROM amazon_security_lake_glue_db_eu_west_1.amazon_security_lake_table_eu_west_1_cloud_trail_mgmt_2_0 WHERE eventday = '20261019' AND accountid = '123456789012' ) TO 's3://my-athena-exports/security-lake/ct-20261019/' WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE') The target prefix must be empty. When the query succeeds, download and combine the files: aws s3 cp s3://my-athena-exports/security-lake/ct-20261019/ ./ct-20261019/ --recursive cat ./ct-20261019/* > securitylake_ct_20261019.jsonl Each line is one OCSF event. To narrow it further, filter on OCSF fields such as api.operation, actor.user.uid or src_endpoint.ip. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Insufficient Lake Formation permissions No SELECT grant on the table Ask the Security Lake admin for a Lake Formation grant Table not found Wrong region in the database or table name Use underscores: eu_west_1 HIVE_PATH_ALREADY_EXISTS or similar Target prefix isn’t empty Use a new, empty prefix Huge scan cost No eventday filter Always filter on partitions Files are gzipped Compression left at the default Set compression = ‘NONE’, or use zcat FAQ Can I read the Parquet files directly? You can, with tools that read Parquet, but Athena handles the schema and partitions for you. For LogTotal, JSON lines from UNLOAD is the simplest route. Is OCSF the same as raw CloudTrail? No. Security Lake normalizes events into OCSF, so field names differ from the original source.

items.title: Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability, Granting Admin Access to Any User
items.summary: IBM has released a security update for a critical IBM Aspera Faspex vulnerability that lets a signed-in user bypass access checks and gain full administrative privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-123218, the flaw affects versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 and carries a CVSS severity score of 9.8. IBM published its security bulletin on November 7, 2026. The supplied CISA catalog entry lists the vulnerability as exploited , with an addition date of November 9 and a remediation deadline of November 12, 2026. It also marks forensic triage as required and ransomware use as unknown. However, we could not independently retrieve the specific entry during verification. IBM’s bulletin does not describe attack campaigns, victims, or exploitation methods beyond a specially crafted message. According to IBM’s security bulletin, an authenticated user can craft a specific message that bypasses user authorization. Successful exploitation gives that user full administrative privileges within Faspex. The advisory does not identify the affected endpoint, message fields, or exact request needed to trigger the flaw. The weakness falls under CWE-863, or incorrect authorization . In simple terms, the software fails to check whether a user has permission to act. Logging in proves who someone is, but authorization should still prevent a standard account from performing tasks reserved for administrators. Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability IBM’s published details show an important mismatch. Its description says the attacker must already be an authorized user. At the same time, its CVSS vector includes “PR: N,” which means no prior privileges are required. Until IBM clarifies this difference, the stated signed-in requirement should guide descriptions of the attack rather than claims that anyone can exploit it without an account. The published score rates potential effects on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability as high. However, the bulletin does not establish that attackers can execute operating system commands or obtain root access. Full Faspex administration and control of the underlying Linux host are different outcomes. Cyber Security News previously covered a separate IBM Aspera Shares vulnerability involving sessions that remained valid after password changes. That issue affected another Aspera product and should not be confused with this Faspex authorization bypass. IBM strongly recommends upgrading affected Linux deployments to Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. Administrators must then verify that the faspex-core container image reports version 5.0.19 with build identifier “1ce4b13” and “Fix Pack: 1.” Checking only the main version number could miss whether the required fix is installed. IBM lists no workarounds or alternative mitigations. Teams should follow the patch instructions linked in the bulletin and confirm the running container contains the corrected image. A deployment still showing version 5.0.19 without the required fix-pack details should not be treated as patched. For defenders following vulnerability news , this case highlights why patch verification matters. Confirming the exact fixed build is essential when vulnerable and corrected releases share the same main version number. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: CVE-2026-125350: Chrome XML Zero-Day Exploited in the Wild
items.summary: Google has released an emergency security update addressing CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity zero-day vulnerability in the XML component of Google Chrome that is already being exploited in real-world attacks. The issue is classified as a use-after-free memory-safety flaw and was reported anonymously to Google on November 6, 2026. Google confirmed on November 9 that an exploit for the vulnerability exists in the wild. However, the company has not disclosed how attackers are delivering the exploit, which organizations or individuals are being targeted, or whether the vulnerability is being chained with additional browser or sandbox escape flaws. Access to the underlying Chromium bug remains restricted while users deploy the security update. The fix is included in Chrome Stable 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. items.title: Turla Hackers Use Cereal Malware Toolset to Exploit Microsoft Exchange Servers for Email Theft
items.summary: Russia-aligned hacking group Turla is using a newly documented malware toolset called Cereal to turn compromised Microsoft Exchange servers into email collection systems and command centers. ESET Research disclosed the findings on November 10, 2026, describing attacks against government organizations in Kazakhstan and Romania. The malware copies selected emails while allowing normal delivery to continue, helping the attackers collect sensitive information without causing an obvious service failure. Turla Hackers Attacking Exchange Servers Researchers first detected the toolset at a Kazakh government organization on November 28, 2025. After improving their detection rules, they identified another compromised government organization in Romania, where activity dated to December 23, 2025. In Romania, the attackers configured the malware to identify messages involving NATO and European Union addresses, including nato.int and europa.eu. These filters point to targeted intelligence collection rather than broad, random email theft. ESET attributed Cereal to Turla with high confidence, citing its use alongside a previously attributed Turla component and similarities to older malware. The group has targeted governments and diplomatic organizations for years. Earlier Cybersecuritynews.com coverage of Turla’s cooperation with Gamaredon described another route to long-term spying, with Gamaredon providing access before Turla deployed its Kazuar backdoor. The researchers could not determine how the attackers initially entered either organization. Although the Exchange servers were internet-facing, exploitation of a software flaw remains only a possibility. The findings do not establish a particular vulnerability, phishing campaign, or stolen account as the entry point. That distinction matters because Cereal describes activity after compromise, not a confirmed new method for breaking into Exchange. Cereal Architecture Overview Diagram (Image Source: ESET Static) Cereal takes its name from serialization, a process for packaging program data so it can later be rebuilt. Its components use this approach to carry encrypted .NET programs, unpack them, and run them in memory. CerealLoader is the only component stored as a recognizable, unencrypted .NET file. Other components arrive inside encrypted containers, reducing the amount of readable malware available for investigators to examine on disk. Exchange Becomes the Command Center According to ESET’s technical white paper , CerealNeuron serves as a passive backdoor. Instead of regularly contacting an outside command server, it waits for incoming requests on the compromised Exchange server. Observed paths include /owa/sdds/ , /AUTODISCOVER/PROXYSERVICE/ , and /MICROSOFT-SERVER-ACTIVESYNC/INTEGRATED/API/ . Their resemblance to normal Exchange services helps malicious requests blend into traffic that organizations need for everyday email access. Requests that pass encryption and integrity checks deliver programs for execution. Invalid requests receive redirects to an Exchange error page. ESET observed no dedicated external command infrastructure and could not identify the operators’ incoming IP addresses. This does not mean the malware has no network activity. Rather, the victim’s server becomes the reachable control point, removing a separate attacker-controlled server that defenders might otherwise identify and block. CerealRunner packages individual tasks as encrypted .NET programs. Observed commands retrieved mail through Exchange Web Services, queried Active Directory, checked processes and connections, extracted locally stored credentials, and managed files. A second backdoor, CerealHermit, reads encrypted commands from disk instead of the network. This use of compromised systems also echoes earlier reporting on Turla’s STOCKSTAY operations , although those attacks involved a different backdoor. CerealBox Delivery Execution Chain (Image Source: ESET Static) The email collection component, CerealBox, runs inside EdgeTransport.exe, which handles Exchange mail flow. Rather than register a new transport agent, it wraps handlers belonging to existing agents in memory. Its code examines messages before returning control to the original handlers. Mail delivery continues, while Exchange’s configuration does not show a newly installed agent. ESET describes this approach to hooking the transport pipeline as previously undocumented in malware. Collection follows specific rules. A message must contain a .doc, .docx, or .pdf attachment and match configured sender, recipient, subject, or attachment-name criteria, while avoiding ignore lists. Selected messages are compressed, encrypted, and stored on disk. Operators then retrieve and delete the staged files using other Cereal commands. The design separates continuous email monitoring from later data removal, allowing the attackers to choose when they collect the results. CerealLoader uses native entry points and VTable Fixups to reach malicious .NET code through execution paths that managed-code inspection can miss. Operators also planted loaders in the .NET native image cache and used DLL search-order hijacking. Together, these techniques show why checking only transport-agent settings or outbound connections would leave important parts of this intrusion unseen during an investigation of compromised Exchange infrastructure and its surrounding Windows systems. items.title: Hackers Exploit Trusted Qubole IAM Roles to Access AWS Accounts and Download Entire S3 Buckets
items.summary: Hackers abused trusted Qubole integrations to enter customer AWS accounts, steal secrets, and download data from Amazon S3, sometimes taking entire buckets in one session. The activity ran from October 14 through October 26, 2026, using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole rather than exploiting a software vulnerability. The attackers relied on permissions customers had granted to the data processing platform. Roles created for legitimate business needs remained accessible even when integrations were no longer active. The case highlights why cloud identity access management requires regular reviews of both permissions and external trust relationships, not simply checks on whether an integration still works. Researchers from Wiz.io, working with Sentra and Mandiant, investigated the campaign after Sentra detected suspicious activity across customer environments. Wiz also identified a malicious bootable Linux image hosted on attacker infrastructure, but could not confirm its deployment or use. items.title: Dark Storm Team Expands DDoS-for-Hire Operations, Demands $5,000 to Stop Alleged Amino Attack
items.summary: Dark Storm Team is combining political attack claims with a growing cybercrime business, advertising distributed denial-of-service services and demanding money to stop alleged disruption. A November 6, 2026, investigation documents its Telegram activity, including a $5,000 cryptocurrency demand linked to the Amino social app. The demand dates to October 2025, rather than a newly confirmed incident. First observed in late 2023, the group gained attention after claiming responsibility for the March 2025 outage affecting X. Its later posts describe attacks against government websites, banks, airports, and online platforms. However, the available evidence does not independently confirm every attack, its duration, or the damage claimed. Researchers from StealthMole identified the commercial operation by tracking Telegram channels, account changes, and messages associated with the persona GLITCH. Their investigation into Dark Storm describes DDoS services and extortion activity, not a newly identified malware family. That distinction matters because the report does not establish which attack software Dark Storm itself deployed. Dark Storm Team Expands DDoS-for-Hire Operations, Demands $5,000 On October 19, 2025, GLITCH posted that the alleged DDoS activity against Amino would stop in exchange for $5,000 in cryptocurrency. A formal attack claim followed on October 22, and the group returned to the target in October 2026. The report does not establish whether Amino paid or independently verify the claimed disruption. The message shows a move beyond selling attacks to customers: the operator publicly used an alleged attack to pressure a target for payment. This sits within the market illustrated by the NightmareStresser DDoS service takedown , where customers could purchase disruptive traffic without building their own attack infrastructure. Dark Storm’s frequently reposted price list offered three hours of DDoS activity for $20, eight hours for $50, one day for $100, one week for $350, and one month for $600. Cryptocurrency was the only advertised payment method. Promotions included an eight-hour service for $25 in late October 2026. The catalogue extended beyond DDoS. A June 2026 menu advertised access to social media accounts starting at $250 and website database dumps from $300. Other advertisements listed database dumping from $50, showing that prices varied between menus. Posts also offered payment card data, CCTV access, and paid channel advertising; these advertisements do not prove successful delivery. GLITCH acted as owner, spokesperson, and sales contact across several accounts. Researchers linked renamed sales handles through a persistent Telegram user ID, allowing them to follow the commercial operation despite changes in its public presentation. This continuity provides stronger evidence of account relationships than matching display names alone. Telegram Resilience, Alliances, and Limits of the Evidence Repeated platform bans did not remove Dark Storm’s presence. Replacement channels appeared throughout 2025 and 2026, while backups and allied communities circulated fresh links. In September 2026, Team1914 helped promote a replacement channel. The pattern adds detail to earlier reporting on pro-Russian hacktivist group alliances involving Dark Storm and other groups. The relationship with Team1914 included reciprocal promotion and joint attack claims. Dark Storm also regularly forwarded NoName057(16) posts and adopted its campaign tags. However, researchers distinguished this amplification from a proven operational partnership. Shared targets, forwarded messages, and overlapping hashtags cannot establish that groups share infrastructure or jointly execute attacks. GLITCH also appeared in a DDoSia Project chat in October 2026 and identified himself as Dark Storm’s owner. Previous reporting on NoName057(16)’s DDoSia attack tool explains its volunteer-driven model, but that appearance does not demonstrate that Dark Storm used the tool. The report leaves the group’s underlying attack infrastructure unresolved. Many attack posts relied on Check-Host availability reports. These show whether selected probes can reach a website, not why access failed. Geographic restrictions, unrelated outages, or defensive filtering may produce similar results. items.summary: .kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.85);}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column482817_d8e68a-90 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information Learn how to check an online seller before you buy Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page. We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them. Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.” None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day. Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35. The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone. These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it. The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings. The stores are copies of one another Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools. The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.” The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number. The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner. What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon. A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership. The videos also depict scenes that don’t appear to be real. Combined with the shared website template and the filename linking two stores, this suggests that one operator or a closely connected group may be involved. It doesn’t establish who is behind the stores. How to spot a questionable store before you pay In our survey earlier this year, 22% of respondents said they had been “misled by AI-generated photos or product reviews.” Here are some checks that can help you spot warning signs. Be wary of endless urgency. If a sale keeps “ending today” or low-stock warnings never change, don’t treat them as proof of a genuine deal. Check that the product could exist. Search the product type and read how the real version works. If the listing claims something the technology can’t do, stop there. Don’t arrive through a link. In this article
  • Store-added reviews and countdowns that keep resetting make products look popular and deals urgent
  • Missing contact details can make it harder to resolve a problem with an order
  • AI-generated images and unverified brand partnerships promote products with no licensing information
  • Learn how to check an online seller before you buy

Advent calendar buying guides are already appearing across the holiday shopping coverage this year. Social media can also put unfamiliar sellers directly in shoppers’ feeds. We found several stores using the same website template, product images with an AI-generated content watermark, and a TikTok account using one store’s branding to link straight to its product page.

We examined stores selling a Legend of Zelda music calendar, a Michael Jackson music calendar, a Lord of the Rings figure calendar, and Harry Potter character plant pots. Other stores, including one selling a Metallica calendar, use the same layout, low-stock warning, and recycled marketing lines. We found no licensing information on the stores, which is reason enough to avoid them.

Fake reviews and countdowns create a false sense of demand

Each store sells a single product. Its page surrounds polished product images with urgency cues: a sale that ends today, a low-stock warning, a five-minute cart reservation timer, a count of orders placed in the last day, and star ratings with thousands of reviews. Testimonials appear underneath, with “verified buyer” badges and timestamps such as “three hours ago.”

None of it is connected to anything. The ratings, review counts, and testimonials are entered into the site theme manually, rather than generated by a review system. The timestamps don’t change, and countdowns reset and run again—on some stores, every day.

Checkout runs through Shopify. That doesn’t establish whether orders will arrive or match their descriptions, and our investigation found no evidence that these pages were designed to steal card details. The risks we can support are misleading sales claims and the possibility of paying for something that never arrives or is very different from what was advertised. Several stores also offer optional checkout add-ons, including shipping protection, a queue-skip fee, and a mystery gift. On one store, these add-ons total nearly $35.

The Zelda calendar’s description contradicts itself

The clearest finding needs no technical analysis. The listing says each of the 25 discs holds a small chip storing your track data, and that the included player reads it and plays music through a built-in speaker with no app, no subscription and no Wi-Fi. Elsewhere on the same page it says the discs work with Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube, and that you can re-link any disc to a new song using a chip-writing app on your phone.

These claims cannot all be true. A device without a network connection can’t stream music from those services. And the instructions for linking discs to new songs suggest that each chip stores a link to a track, rather than the track itself. That’s how the legitimate version of this product works, according to our research: the chip holds a link, and a phone plays the music. Someone appears to have copied that mechanism and bolted a fictional standalone speaker onto it.

The bundle pricing also doesn’t add up. Two bundles claim savings of $15 and $33, but the prices shown below them work out to about $19 and $43 in savings.

The stores are copies of one another

Despite their different names, the stores we examined are nearly identical. They use the same commercial theme version and share an internal fingerprint indicating that their theme files are copies of one another. They also block right-clicking and access to developer tools.

The most direct link was left behind by accident, in that one store’s theme is still named after the file it was exported from, and that filename includes the web address of another store in the group. Other pages contain leftover text from a previous shop, including a warranty promising to replace costumes that don’t inflate properly and a scrolling banner with the unedited placeholder “use code X for X percent off.”

The stores’ files are timestamped from mid-July to the second week of September, with the newest store only days old when we examined it. Most merchant accounts are registered in Romania, while prices are shown in dollars. None of the calendar stores we examined listed a business address or phone number.

The pattern runs well past unlicensed character merchandise. We found advent calendars for fishing lures, squishy toys, charm bracelets, and wearable jumpers, with the same countdowns, stock warnings, and paid add-ons. Most appear to sell real, inexpensive goods at a steep markup. Their add-on prices differ, so we can’t conclude that the same person runs all of them. The evidence points to a shared sales playbook, not necessarily a shared owner.

What the evidence shows, and what it doesn’t

Product images from two of the calendar stores triggered a provenance checker for a watermark, indicating they were produced with OpenAI tools. The filenames agree: across three stores every product image follows the same automated naming pattern, and one store’s entire photography set is timestamped to a single afternoon.

A TikTok account uses one store’s name and branding and links directly to its product page. Several videos claim the store is collaborating with Walmart. They show retail scenes, including an oversized character figure outside a store and pallets of branded boxes. We found no evidence of such a partnership. The videos also depict scenes that don’t appear to be real. Combined with the shared website template and the filename linking two stores, this suggests that one operator or a closely connected group may be involved. It doesn’t establish who is behind the stores.

How to spot a questionable store before you pay

In our survey earlier this year, 22% of respondents said they had been “misled by AI-generated photos or product reviews.”
Here are some checks that can help you spot warning signs.

  • Be wary of endless urgency. If a sale keeps “ending today” or low-stock warnings never change, don’t treat them as proof of a genuine deal.
  • Check that the product could exist. Search the product type and read how the real version works. If the listing claims something the technology can’t do, stop there.
  • Don’t arrive through a link. These stores sell largely through social video. Search the brand name separately and look for history, press, or customers outside its own website.
  • Treat partnership claims as claims. A video saying a brand is stocked by a retailer isn’t evidence that it is. Partnerships are announced by the retailer too, not only by the seller.
  • Look for a real business. A postal address, company registration and working phone number are easy for a legitimate seller to provide and were absent from these.

  • Read the small print against itself. If a calendar’s warranty talks about inflatable costumes, the page wasn’t written for the product you’re buying.
  • Check the spelling, including on the box. We found a misspelled artist name in a product title, a mangled savings line, and a calendar with the word spelled “calindar” on the packaging artwork itself. A real manufacturer proofreads its own box.
  • Pay with a method that offers buyer protection. A credit card or payment service with buyer protection gives you a route to a refund. Bank transfers can be harder to reverse.

items.title: Hackers Breach Fireworks AI Through Third-Party Cloud Provider to Steal Customer Data
items.summary: Fireworks AI has disclosed a wider security breach involving customer account details, billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. In a November 9, 2026 update, the company said attackers reached its development machines through a third-party cloud provider, expanding the impact beyond the exposed credentials reported in October. The findings change the picture presented in its first disclosure. Fireworks initially reported unauthorized access to secrets used in evaluation jobs across a limited number of accounts. Its latest investigation confirms access to additional customer information, including portions of unfinished models and datasets belonging to certain customers. Fireworks AI Data Breach The newly disclosed attack path began on October 23, when a cloud provider hosting Fireworks research and development machines experienced a security incident. On October 24, an unauthorized party used that opening to access Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload, causing further customer data exposure. Fireworks said it detected the activity that day, took immediate response measures, and closed known critical vulnerabilities. The company has not named the cloud provider or disclosed specific vulnerabilities. It reported no further detected successful access by the attacker on its customer platform as of October 25. The earlier incident began on October 6, when Fireworks detected misuse of internal credentials. Attackers accessed environment variables used by evaluation jobs, potentially capturing API keys and tokens. Fireworks began customer notifications on October 7 and later revoked affected keys, employee credentials, and service-account tokens. According to the updated security bulletin , the affected internal application exposed resource identifiers, names, descriptions, and creation times. Billing information included billing and shipping addresses, invoices, payment history, balances, and credit usage. Fireworks does not store payment card numbers and said those numbers were unaffected. For certain customers, attackers accessed a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets. The disclosure does not establish theft of complete production models. Fireworks also reported no detected impact to Inference, Training SDK, or Nexus, which operate with zero data retention by default. Its investigation remains ongoing. Fireworks said evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to sell unauthorized access to large language models through illicit routing gateways, known as LLMJacking. Cybersecurity News previously covered LLMHijacking attacks and large cloud bills , explaining how stolen cloud credentials enable resale of paid AI services. The company has notified law enforcement and brought in Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic support. Its response includes replacing credentials, reducing elevated permissions, isolating affected systems, and tightening storage access. Related reporting on cloud credential theft using autonomous AI agents highlights the broader risk around compromised cloud accounts. Fireworks has disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads for Batch Inference and dataset-based training during the investigation. Training SDK remains available, while Fireworks Lab-based training runs in an isolated environment with added network and storage protection. The company is directly notifying customers whose data was affected. Its original customer guidance advises affected users to replace revoked Fireworks keys and rotate exposed third-party credentials with their issuing providers. Deleting a stored secret does not invalidate the underlying credential. Customers should also review access logs, unfamiliar users, API keys, training jobs, and datasets for unauthorized activity. items.title: Terminal2Shell: 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ Dating Back to 1971 Claims to Affect Billions of Devices
items.summary: Terminal2Shell claims a critical flaw dating back to 1971 affects more than two billion devices, allowing anyone who opens a terminal to gain an interactive shell. However, the website is satire, not a confirmed vulnerability disclosure. Its “exploit” describes normal terminal use, making it a joke about security marketing rather than a newly discovered threat. The page calls the issue “TermGeddon,” lists its CVE as pending, and claims a CVSS score of 11.0 out of 10. That score is an immediate warning sign because the official CVSS scale stops at 10.0. Claims about billions of affected devices should therefore not be treated as verified findings. Terminal2Shell 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ The supposed attack requires local access, a keyboard, and the ability to open a terminal. It then gives the person the permissions of the account already signed in. Nothing in this description demonstrates an authentication bypass, remote compromise, or access to another user’s account. The claimed attack simply starts with access the person already has. This distinction matters. A shell provides a way to enter commands. A security flaw must do more than show that commands run when an authorized user types them. Terminal2Shell presents expected behavior as a critical discovery, using alarming labels and a branded website to make an ordinary feature sound dangerous. For readers, the useful question is not whether a demonstration opens a shell. It is who controls that shell, what access they needed beforehand, and whether the attack crosses a security boundary. Terminal2Shell’s own description fails that test because the user already has the access being “obtained.” How Real Shell Exploits Differ The Terminal2Shell website contrasts sharply with Able2Shell . N-able took hosted N-central servers offline after reports of 33 alleged vulnerabilities and published exploit code. Huntress identified four exploit chains, including three leading to remote code execution. Unlike opening your own terminal, these chains involve attackers gaining control through weaknesses in management software. Plex2Shell shows why that difference matters. Attackers reportedly used a chain of Plex flaws to install cryptocurrency miners shortly after exploit code became public. The reported fixed release is Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861. Users should check their installed version rather than assume an exposed server remains safe because it works normally. PHP2Shell involved another important distinction: gaining an initial foothold is not always the final step. Researchers reported attackers combining it with a Linux kernel flaw to obtain root access on 25 servers. Updating an application alone would not address a separate weakness in the underlying operating system. HTTP2Shell and Node2Shell concern a Brotli decoding flaw, not ordinary command entry. Reported effects differ across affected software, including crashes and demonstrated code execution. Node.js users should check the fixed releases listed in the coverage: 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. A shared component does not mean every affected product has an identical attack path. WP2Shell reportedly allows attackers to create WordPress administrator accounts and install web shells without signing in. That missing login requirement marks a real security boundary being crossed. The coverage identifies WordPress 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed releases. Terminal2Shell needs no emergency patch based on its stated behavior. Its practical lesson is to separate dramatic branding from evidence: identify the affected product, required access, demonstrated impact, and available fix before treating a claim as an incident. Terminal2Shell’s own description fails that test because the user already has the access being “obtained.”

How Real Shell Exploits Differ

The Terminal2Shell website contrasts sharply with Able2Shell. N-able took hosted N-central servers offline after reports of 33 alleged vulnerabilities and published exploit code.

Huntress identified four exploit chains, including three leading to remote code execution. Unlike opening your own terminal, these chains involve attackers gaining control through weaknesses in management software.

Plex2Shell shows why that difference matters. Attackers reportedly used a chain of Plex flaws to install cryptocurrency miners shortly after exploit code became public. The reported fixed release is Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861. Users should check their installed version rather than assume an exposed server remains safe because it works normally.

PHP2Shell involved another important distinction: gaining an initial foothold is not always the final step. Researchers reported attackers combining it with a Linux kernel flaw to obtain root access on 25 servers. Updating an application alone would not address a separate weakness in the underlying operating system.

HTTP2Shell and Node2Shell concern a Brotli decoding flaw, not ordinary command entry. Reported effects differ across affected software, including crashes and demonstrated code execution. Node.js users should check the fixed releases listed in the coverage: 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. A shared component does not mean every affected product has an identical attack path.

WP2Shell reportedly allows attackers to create WordPress administrator accounts and install web shells without signing in. That missing login requirement marks a real security boundary being crossed. The coverage identifies WordPress 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed releases.

Terminal2Shell needs no emergency patch based on its stated behavior. Its practical lesson is to separate dramatic branding from evidence: identify the affected product, required access, demonstrated impact, and available fix before treating a claim as an incident.

items.title: N-able Takes N-central Servers Offline Worldwide After 33 0-Day Vulnerabilities and Able2Shell Exploits
items.summary: N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline on November 9, 2026, after an independent researcher published details of 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities and exploit code. The company also told customers running N-central on their own servers to take them offline until further notice, creating an outage for users of its remote monitoring and management platform. The shutdown covers hosted services across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. N-able said the move was a precaution while its teams worked on a hotfix. As of November 9 at 15:15 UTC, the company said it had not seen active exploitation. Customers were told not to restore servers until N-able confirms they can safely return online. The public release, called Able2Shell, contains technical writeups and proof-of-concept code. Huntress reported that the 33 disclosed issues can form four separate exploit chains. Three lead to remote code execution, allowing commands to run on a vulnerable server. The fourth enables privilege escalation to root, the most powerful account on the underlying operating system. The research targets N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, with earlier versions also potentially affected. However, the full scope remains unconfirmed. Censys noted that N-able had not published an affected-version list, fixed versions, CVE identifiers, or severity scores for these newly disclosed issues as of November 9. The reported count should therefore remain distinct from a vendor-validated vulnerability list. N-central gives managed service providers a central place to monitor devices, install patches, run scripts, and support customer systems. That access makes a server compromise especially serious. Earlier N-central authentication bypass attacks showed how attackers could use the platform’s Take Control feature to reach managed devices. Those previous incidents are separate from Able2Shell. Able2Shell Exploit Chains Allow Server Takeover According to Field Effect’s analysis , the disclosure includes both authenticated and unauthenticated weaknesses. Claimed impacts include command execution, credential exposure, administrator account creation, configuration changes, and audit record manipulation. One published Python proof of concept describes an XML External Entity, or XXE, flaw that can be chained into remote code execution without a login. An XXE flaw occurs when an application processes unsafe references inside XML data. In this case, researchers describe it as an entry point into a broader server takeover chain. However, the public release should not be treated as proof that every claimed issue works across every installation. Censys cautioned that N-able’s notice did not confirm the individual mechanisms or impacts. The incident follows earlier N-central security problems, including an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-86218. That flaw received a September hotfix. It is not an Able2Shell identifier, and installing an earlier security update does not establish protection against this new disclosure. Customers need guidance specific to the current incident. Some management functions remain available despite the classic N-central outage. N-able’s notice directs eligible customers to its separate application portal using N-able Login. The application documentation describes asset views, patch management, vulnerability management, scripts, policies, and tags. Availability depends on permissions, licensing, and configuration. Take Control through this portal currently supports Windows devices, not macOS. For defenders, Huntress recommends reviewing login and authentication activity from November 8 onward. Teams should investigate unexpected administrator accounts, unusual remote access sessions, and newly deployed scripts. Suspicious activity should trigger an incident response review that includes customer networks managed through the affected server, rather than stopping at the N-central appliance itself. Recovery should follow N-able’s instructions, not simply the appearance of an update. Huntress noted that live hotfixes may not change the displayed version number. Administrators should keep servers offline, confirm that the required fix has been applied, and wait for explicit clearance before restoring access to production management services.

Weekly Update 529: Kids Social Media Bans (and Everything Else)
items.summary: The kids-and-social-media discussion is just dumb. It's not the premise of delaying their access until 16, but the inability of those who should know better to grasp where the responsibility for enforcement lies. Here's our PM's explainer after the laws passed down here a couple of years ago: The onus won't be on parents or young people. There will be no penalties for users. And it's been expressed many times since, in similar terms, always to the effect of placing responsibility for implementation and enforcement on the social media platforms. Inevitably, there are some massive holes in their implementation, along with major privacy and social concerns. But as I say this week (and have said on many previous occasions), it doesn't have to be perfect; over the long run, it will gradually change social norms, and the kids in that shoulder age bracket right now will have a different set of expectations than those who come after them. But hopefully, in the interim, the whole "onus won't be on parents" mantra will be respected more than it has been to date.
